10: ## About Laravel
11: 
12: Laravel is a web application framework with expressive, elegant syntax. We believe development must be an enjoyable and creative experience to be truly fulfilling. Laravel takes the pain out of development by easing common tasks used in many web projects, such as:
13: 
14: - [Simple, fast routing engine](https://laravel.com/docs/routing).
15: - [Powerful dependency injection container](https://laravel.com/docs/container).
16: - Multiple back-ends for [session](https://laravel.com/docs/session) and [cache](https://laravel.com/docs/cache) storage.
17: - Expressive, intuitive [database ORM](https://laravel.com/docs/eloquent).
18: - Database agnostic [schema migrations](https://laravel.com/docs/migrations).
19: - [Robust background job processing](https://laravel.com/docs/queues).
20: - [Real-time event broadcasting](https://laravel.com/docs/broadcasting).
21: 
22: Laravel is accessible, powerful, and provides tools required for large, robust applications.
23: 
24: ## Learning Laravel
25: 
26: Laravel has the most extensive and thorough [documentation](https://laravel.com/docs) and video tutorial library of all modern web application frameworks, making it a breeze to get started with the framework.
27: 
28: In addition, [Laracasts](https://laracasts.com) contains thousands of video tutorials on a range of topics including Laravel, modern PHP, unit testing, and JavaScript. Boost your skills by digging into our comprehensive video library.
29: 
30: You can also watch bite-sized lessons with real-world projects on [Laravel Learn](https://laravel.com/learn), where you will be guided through building a Laravel application from scratch while learning PHP fundamentals.
31: 
32: ## Agentic Development
33: 
34: Laravel's predictable structure and conventions make it ideal for AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Install [Laravel Boost](https://laravel.com/docs/ai) to supercharge your AI workflow:
35: 
36: ```bash
37: composer require laravel/boost --dev
38: 
39: php artisan boost:install
40: ```
41: 
42: Boost provides your agent 15+ tools and skills that help agents build Laravel applications while following best practices.
43: 
44: ## Contributing
45: 
46: Thank you for considering contributing to the Laravel framework! The contribution guide can be found in the [Laravel documentation](https://laravel.com/docs/contributions).
47: 
48: ## Code of Conduct
49: 
50: In order to ensure that the Laravel community is welcoming to all, please review and abide by the [Code of Conduct](https://laravel.com/docs/contributions#code-of-conduct).
51: 
52: ## Security Vulnerabilities
53: 
54: If you discover a security vulnerability within Laravel, please send an e-mail to Taylor Otwell via [taylor@laravel.com](mailto:taylor@laravel.com). All security vulnerabilities will be promptly addressed.
55:

Exploration complete. Here's an overview of the project:

## Incite Academy — English Learning Platform (TOEFL-prep LMS)

### Stack
| Layer | Technology |
|---|---|
| Backend | Laravel 13.38, PHP 8.5, SQLite |
| Frontend | Inertia v3 (SSR) + React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Vite 8 |
| Auth | Laravel Breeze (Inertia) + Google OAuth via Socialite (commit says "incomplete") |
| Testing | Pest 5 (PHP) + Vitest 5 (JS), Playwright for screenshots |
| Tooling | Pint, ESLint/Prettier, Laravel Boost, Ziggy |

### Domain Model
`MajorDepartement` → `User`, and `Course` → `Module` → `Lesson` → `Question` → `Answer`

- **Course**: title, category (Reading / Listening / Structure & Writing — the three TOEFL sections), denormalized stats (`modules_count`, `lessons_count`, `total_duration`, `total_points`) recalculated via `recalculateStats()`
- **Lesson**: typed as `article`, `quiz`, or `exam`; auto-computes points (words/10 for articles, 10×questions for quizzes) and duration (reading time, audio time via `audio_duration`)
- **User**: `role` (admin/student), `academic_status` (Indonesian: `Mahasiswa`), `nim_nip` (student/staff ID) — this is an Indonesian university context
- Storage hygiene: models track `storedFilePaths()` for safe deletion of cover images and question audio on the public disk

### Application Structure
- **Public**: `/` Welcome landing page, `/home` student home (minimal)
- **Admin** (`auth` + `verified` + `admin` middleware): `/dashboard` with Overview, Courses CRUD with nested module/lesson editors (scoped bindings, drag-and-drop reordering via dnd-kit, TipTap WYSIWYG, audio uploads), Users management
- **Auth**: full Breeze suite (login, register, verify email, password reset) + `GoogleAuthController`

### Frontend Conventions
- Pages in `resources/js/Pages/<Area>/index.jsx`, shared layouts (`AdminLayout`, `AuthLayout`), ~40 reusable components, zustand store (`useCourseDraftStore`), react-hook-form + zod validation (`zodRules.js`), a leftover `resources/oldjs/` from a redesign

### Current State (git log)
Work is tracked as F-## tickets. Recently finished **F-31** (course management page + full DB schema). Before that: F-26–F-29 (admin users CRUD), F-02/F-03/F-04 (Google OAuth, role-based redirects, admin guard). Latest commit refactored zod rules to be importable.

### Notable Gaps / Observations
1. Google OAuth login is incomplete (F-02)
2. No student-facing course-taking flow yet (enrollment, lesson viewing, quiz answering — the Answer/Question schema exists but only the admin side is built)
3. `MajorDepartement` is a misspelling of "Department", but it's the established convention throughout migrations/models/factories
4. Tests cover auth, profile, dashboard access, and users/courses management; no tests yet for lessons/modules

```

All recipes in LessonContent.jsx are arrow functions with block bodies that mutate `draft` and return `undefined`:

});
```

So `recipe(...)` returns `undefined` → `next` is `undefined` → `next.article_content` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'article_content')`.

The comment says "LessonContent mutates nested arrays/properties via an Immer-style draft recipe" — the code was clearly meant to use Immer's `produce(base, recipe)` which returns the next state even when the recipe returns undefined. Immer is already a dependency in package.json (`immer: ^11.2.10`). So the fix is:

```js
import { produce } from 'immer';
...

```

With Immer, you don't even need `structuredClone` — produce handles the draft. Also `structuredClone` would throw on File objects anyway (structuredClone can clone File objects actually — File is cloneable via structuredClone. Yes, Files can be structured-cloned. But blobs work too. Actually structuredClone supports File and Blob). But produce is cleaner and matches the comment.

Found it. Here's the full diagnosis:

## Root Cause

**`resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Lessons/Editor/index.jsx` — `handleLessonUpdate`, line 62:**

```js
const current = getValues();
const next = recipe(structuredClone(current));  // ← recipe returns undefined!
```

Every recipe passed to `update()` from `LessonContent.jsx` mutates its `draft` argument and **returns nothing** (block-bodied arrow with no `return`), e.g. line 176:

```js
update((draft) => {
    draft.article_content = html;
});
```

So `recipe(...)` returns `undefined` → `next` is `undefined` → line 65 `next.article_content` throws your exact error. The mutations do land on the clone, but the return value is what's used.

Two telling details:
- The comments say *"Immer-style draft recipe"* and LessonContent's docblock says *"the Immer-backed `update` helper"* — the design intent was Immer's `produce(base, recipe)`, where the recipe mutates a proxy draft and `produce` returns the next state. **The actual `produce()` call was never wired in.**
- `immer@11.2.10` is already in `package.json` dependencies but imported nowhere — it was added for exactly this.

Note this isn't just the article editor: the **quiz/exam branch is equally broken** — question edits would crash at `next.questions` (line 70) / `next.questions.length` (line 75). The first keystroke in any WysiwygEditor triggers it.

## Proposed Fix (one line + one import)

In `resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Lessons/Editor/index.jsx`:

```js
import { produce } from 'immer';
// ...
const next = produce(current, recipe);  // replaces recipe(structuredClone(current))
```

`produce(current, recipe)` returns the next state even when the recipe returns `undefined`, mutating only what the recipe touched. This single funnel fixes **all** update recipes (article content, question add/delete/edit, audio upload/remove, reordering).

Why this is safe here:
- `structuredClone` is no longer needed (produce makes the copy)
- File objects in `questions[].audio_file` pass through by reference (non-draftable), so multipart submission keeps working
- The produced state is frozen by default, but every consumer is read-only (`AnswerChoicesInput` uses spread/map/filter; `WysiwygEditor` only reads)

Then run `npm run test` (vitest) to confirm nothing regressed. No new test is practical without adding a DOM test environment (happy-dom + @testing-library/react), which would change dev dependencies — I can do that separately with your approval.

**Alternative** (zero new imports): `const next = structuredClone(current); recipe(next);` — mutates the clone in place and uses it. Works, but abandons the documented Immer intent and leaves `immer` unused.

<skill_content name="inertia-react-development">
# Skill: inertia-react-development

# Inertia React Development

## When to Apply

Activate this skill when:

- Creating or modifying React page components for Inertia
- Working with forms in React (using `<Form>`, `useForm`, or `useHttp`)
- Implementing client-side navigation with `<Link>` or `router`
- Using v3 features: deferred props, prefetching, optimistic updates, instant visits, layout props, HTTP requests, WhenVisible, InfiniteScroll, once props, flash data, or polling
- Building React-specific features with the Inertia protocol

## Documentation

Use `search-docs` for detailed Inertia v3 React patterns and documentation.

## Basic Usage

### Page Components Location

React page components should be placed in the `resources/js/Pages` directory.

### Page Component Structure

<!-- Basic React Page Component -->
```react
export default function UsersIndex({ users }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Users</h1>
            <ul>
                {users.map(user => <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>)}
            </ul>
        </div>
    )
}
```

## Client-Side Navigation

### Basic Link Component

Use `<Link>` for client-side navigation instead of traditional `<a>` tags:

<!-- Inertia React Navigation -->
```react
import { Link, router } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Link href="/">Home</Link>
<Link href="/users">Users</Link>
<Link href={`/users/${user.id}`}>View User</Link>
```

### Link with Method

<!-- Link with POST Method -->
```react
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Link href="/logout" method="post" as="button">
    Logout
</Link>
```

### Prefetching

Prefetch pages to improve perceived performance:

<!-- Prefetch on Hover -->
```react
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Link href="/users" prefetch>
    Users
</Link>
```

### Programmatic Navigation

<!-- Router Visit -->
```react
import { router } from '@inertiajs/react'

function handleClick() {
    router.visit('/users')
}

// Or with options
router.visit('/users', {
    method: 'post',
    data: { name: 'John' },
    onSuccess: () => console.log('Success!'),
})
```

## Form Handling

### Form Component (Recommended)

The recommended way to build forms is with the `<Form>` component:

<!-- Form Component Example -->
```react
import { Form } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function CreateUser() {
    return (
        <Form action="/users" method="post">
            {({ errors, processing, wasSuccessful }) => (
                <>
                    <input type="text" name="name" />
                    {errors.name && <div>{errors.name}</div>}

                    <input type="email" name="email" />
                    {errors.email && <div>{errors.email}</div>}

                    <button type="submit" disabled={processing}>
                        {processing ? 'Creating...' : 'Create User'}
                    </button>

                    {wasSuccessful && <div>User created!</div>}
                </>
            )}
        </Form>
    )
}
```

### Form Component With All Props

<!-- Form Component Full Example -->
```react
import { Form } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Form action="/users" method="post">
    {({
        errors,
        hasErrors,
        processing,
        progress,
        wasSuccessful,
        recentlySuccessful,
        clearErrors,
        resetAndClearErrors,
        defaults,
        isDirty,
        reset,
        submit
    }) => (
        <>
            <input type="text" name="name" defaultValue={defaults.name} />
            {errors.name && <div>{errors.name}</div>}

            <button type="submit" disabled={processing}>
                {processing ? 'Saving...' : 'Save'}
            </button>

            {progress && (
                <progress value={progress.percentage} max="100">
                    {progress.percentage}%
                </progress>
            )}

            {wasSuccessful && <div>Saved!</div>}
        </>
    )}
</Form>
```

### Form Component Reset Props

The `<Form>` component supports automatic resetting:

- `resetOnError` - Reset form data when the request fails
- `resetOnSuccess` - Reset form data when the request succeeds
- `setDefaultsOnSuccess` - Update default values on success

Use the `search-docs` tool with a query of `form component resetting` for detailed guidance.

<!-- Form with Reset Props -->
```react
import { Form } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Form
    action="/users"
    method="post"
    resetOnSuccess
    setDefaultsOnSuccess
>
    {({ errors, processing, wasSuccessful }) => (
        <>
            <input type="text" name="name" />
            {errors.name && <div>{errors.name}</div>}

            <button type="submit" disabled={processing}>
                Submit
            </button>
        </>
    )}
</Form>
```

Forms can also be built using the `useForm` helper for more programmatic control. Use the `search-docs` tool with a query of `useForm helper` for guidance.

### `useForm` Hook

For more programmatic control or to follow existing conventions, use the `useForm` hook:

<!-- useForm Hook Example -->
```react
import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function CreateUser() {
    const { data, setData, post, processing, errors, reset } = useForm({
        name: '',
        email: '',
        password: '',
    })

    function submit(e) {
        e.preventDefault()
        post('/users', {
            onSuccess: () => reset('password'),
        })
    }

    return (
        <form onSubmit={submit}>
            <input
                type="text"
                value={data.name}
                onChange={e => setData('name', e.target.value)}
            />
            {errors.name && <div>{errors.name}</div>}

            <input
                type="email"
                value={data.email}
                onChange={e => setData('email', e.target.value)}
            />
            {errors.email && <div>{errors.email}</div>}

            <input
                type="password"
                value={data.password}
                onChange={e => setData('password', e.target.value)}
            />
            {errors.password && <div>{errors.password}</div>}

            <button type="submit" disabled={processing}>
                Create User
            </button>
        </form>
    )
}
```

## Inertia v3 Features

### HTTP Requests

Use the `useHttp` hook for standalone HTTP requests that do not trigger Inertia page visits. It provides the same developer experience as `useForm`, but for plain JSON endpoints.

<!-- useHttp Example -->
```react
import { useHttp } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Search() {
    const { data, setData, get, processing } = useHttp({
        query: '',
    })

    function search(e) {
        setData('query', e.target.value)
        get('/api/search', {
            onSuccess: (response) => {
                console.log(response)
            },
        })
    }

    return (
        <>
            <input value={data.query} onChange={search} />
            {processing && <div>Searching...</div>}
        </>
    )
}
```

### Optimistic Updates

Apply data changes instantly before the server responds, with automatic rollback on failure:

<!-- Optimistic Update with Router -->
```react
import { router } from '@inertiajs/react'

function like(post) {
    router.optimistic((props) => ({
        post: {
            ...props.post,
            likes: props.post.likes + 1,
        },
    })).post(`/posts/${post.id}/like`)
}
```

Optimistic updates also work with `useForm` and the `<Form>` component:

<!-- Optimistic Update with Form Component -->
```react
import { Form } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Form
    action="/todos"
    method="post"
    optimistic={(props, data) => ({
        todos: [...props.todos, { id: Date.now(), name: data.name, done: false }],
    })}
>
    <input type="text" name="name" />
    <button type="submit">Add Todo</button>
</Form>
```

### Instant Visits

Navigate to a new page immediately without waiting for the server response. The target component renders right away with shared props, while page-specific props load in the background.

<!-- Instant Visit with Link -->
```react
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react'

<Link href="/dashboard" component="Dashboard">Dashboard</Link>

<Link
    href="/posts/1"
    component="Posts/Show"
    pageProps={{ post: { id: 1, title: 'My Post' } }}
>
    View Post
</Link>
```

### Layout Props

Share dynamic data between pages and persistent layouts:

<!-- Layout Props in Layout -->
```react
export default function Layout({ title = 'My App', showSidebar = true, children }) {
    return (
        <>
            <header>{title}</header>
            {showSidebar && <aside>Sidebar</aside>}
            <main>{children}</main>
        </>
    )
}
```

<!-- Setting Layout Props from Page -->
```react
import { setLayoutProps } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Dashboard() {
    setLayoutProps({
        title: 'Dashboard',
        showSidebar: false,
    })

    return <h1>Dashboard</h1>
}
```

### Deferred Props

Use deferred props to load data after initial page render:

<!-- Deferred Props with Empty State -->
```react
export default function UsersIndex({ users }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Users</h1>
            {!users ? (
                <div className="animate-pulse">
                    <div className="h-4 bg-gray-200 rounded w-3/4 mb-2"></div>
                    <div className="h-4 bg-gray-200 rounded w-1/2"></div>
                </div>
            ) : (
                <ul>
                    {users.map(user => (
                        <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
                    ))}
                </ul>
            )}
        </div>
    )
}
```

### Polling

Use the `usePoll` hook to automatically refresh data at intervals. It handles cleanup on unmount and throttles polling when the tab is inactive.

<!-- Basic Polling -->
```react
import { usePoll } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Dashboard({ stats }) {
    usePoll(5000)

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Dashboard</h1>
            <div>Active Users: {stats.activeUsers}</div>
        </div>
    )
}
```

<!-- Polling With Request Options and Manual Control -->
```react
import { usePoll } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Dashboard({ stats }) {
    const { start, stop } = usePoll(5000, {
        only: ['stats'],
        onStart() {
            console.log('Polling request started')
        },
        onFinish() {
            console.log('Polling request finished')
        },
    }, {
        autoStart: false,
        keepAlive: true,
    })

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Dashboard</h1>
            <div>Active Users: {stats.activeUsers}</div>
            <button onClick={start}>Start Polling</button>
            <button onClick={stop}>Stop Polling</button>
        </div>
    )
}
```

- `autoStart` (default `true`) - set to `false` to start polling manually via the returned `start()` function
- `keepAlive` (default `false`) - set to `true` to prevent throttling when the browser tab is inactive

### WhenVisible

Lazy-load a prop when an element scrolls into view. Useful for deferring expensive data that sits below the fold:

<!-- WhenVisible Example -->
```react
import { WhenVisible } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Dashboard({ stats }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Dashboard</h1>

            <WhenVisible data="stats" buffer={200} fallback={<div className="animate-pulse">Loading stats...</div>}>
                {({ fetching }) => (
                    <div>
                        <p>Total Users: {stats.total_users}</p>
                        <p>Revenue: {stats.revenue}</p>
                        {fetching && <span>Refreshing...</span>}
                    </div>
                )}
            </WhenVisible>
        </div>
    )
}
```

### InfiniteScroll

Automatically load additional pages of paginated data as users scroll:

<!-- InfiniteScroll Example -->
```react
import { InfiniteScroll } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Users({ users }) {
    return (
        <InfiniteScroll data="users">
            {users.data.map(user => (
                <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
            ))}
        </InfiniteScroll>
    )
}
```

The server must use `Inertia::scroll()` to configure the paginated data. Use the `search-docs` tool with a query of `infinite scroll` for detailed guidance on buffers, manual loading, reverse mode, and custom trigger elements.

## Server-Side Patterns

Server-side patterns (Inertia::render, props, middleware) are covered in inertia-laravel guidelines.

## Common Pitfalls

- Using traditional `<a>` links instead of Inertia's `<Link>` component (breaks SPA behavior)
- Forgetting to add loading states (skeleton screens) when using deferred props
- Not handling the `undefined` state of deferred props before data loads
- Using `<form>` without preventing default submission (use `<Form>` component or `e.preventDefault()`)
- Forgetting to check if `<Form>` component is available in your Inertia version
- Using `router.cancel()` instead of `router.cancelAll()` (v3 breaking change)
- Using `router.on('invalid', ...)` or `router.on('exception', ...)` instead of the renamed `httpException` and `networkError` events

139:     public function update(LessonUpdateRequest $request, Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson): RedirectResponse
140:     {
141:         $validated = $request->validated();
142:         $type = $validated['type'];
143:         $previousAudioPaths = $lesson->storedAudioPaths();
144:         $existingQuestions = $lesson->questions()->get()->keyBy('id');
145:         $keptAudioPaths = [];
146: 
147:         DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $module, $lesson, $validated, $type, $existingQuestions, &$keptAudioPaths): void {
148:             $lesson->update([
149:                 'title' => $validated['title'],
150:                 'type' => $type,
151:                 'article_content' => $type === 'article' ? ($validated['article_content'] ?? '') : null,
152:                 'duration' => $type === 'exam' ? (int) $validated['duration'] : 0,
153:             ]);
154: 
155:             $lesson->questions()->delete();
156: 
157:             if ($type !== 'article') {
158:                 $keptAudioPaths = $this->syncQuestions(
159:                     $lesson,
160:                     $validated['questions'] ?? [],
161:                     $existingQuestions,
162:                 );
163:             }
164: 
165:             $lesson->load('questions');
166:             $lesson->recalculatePoints();
167:             $lesson->recalculateDuration();
168:             $module->recalculateStats();
169:             $course->recalculateStats();
170:         });
171: 
172:         $orphanedPaths = array_diff($previousAudioPaths, $keptAudioPaths);
173: 
174:         if ($orphanedPaths !== []) {
175:             Storage::disk('public')->delete(array_values($orphanedPaths));
176:         }
177: 
178:         return redirect()->route('dashboard.courses.edit', $course);
179:     }

213:     /**
214:      * Persist ordered questions and answers, returning any retained audio paths.
215:      *
216:      * @param  array<int, array<string, mixed>>  $questionsData
217:      * @param  Collection<int, Question>  $existingQuestions
218:      * @return array<int, string>
219:      */
220:     private function syncQuestions(Lesson $lesson, array $questionsData, $existingQuestions): array
221:     {
222:         $keptAudioPaths = [];
223: 
224:         foreach ($questionsData as $questionIdx => $questionData) {
225:             $questionType = $questionData['type'];
226:             $audioUrl = null;
227:             $audioDuration = null;
228: 
229:             if ($questionType === 'listening') {
230:                 $audioDuration = isset($questionData['audio_duration'])
231:                     ? (int) round((float) $questionData['audio_duration'])
232:                     : null;
233: 
234:                 if (($questionData['audio_file'] ?? null) instanceof UploadedFile) {
235:                     $audioUrl = $questionData['audio_file']->store('lessons/audio', 'public');
236:                 } elseif (! empty($questionData['audio_url']) && isset($questionData['id'])) {
237:                     $existingAudio = $existingQuestions->get((int) $questionData['id'])?->audio_url;
238: 
239:                     if ($existingAudio) {
240:                         $audioUrl = $existingAudio;
241:                         $keptAudioPaths[] = $existingAudio;
242:                     }
243:                 }
244:             }
245: 
246:             $question = $lesson->questions()->create([
247:                 'type' => $questionType,
248:                 'question_content' => $questionData['question_content'],
249:                 'audio_url' => $audioUrl,
250:                 'audio_duration' => $audioDuration,
251:                 'order_index' => $questionIdx,
252:             ]);
253: 
254:             $answers = [];
255: 
256:             foreach ($questionData['answers'] as $answerIdx => $answerContent) {
257:                 $answers[$answerIdx] = $question->answers()->create([
258:                     'answer_content' => $answerContent,
259:                     'order_index' => $answerIdx,
260:                 ]);
261:             }
262: 
263:             $question->update([
264:                 'correct_answer_id' => $answers[(int) $questionData['correct_answer_index']]->id,
265:             ]);
266:         }
267: 
268:         return $keptAudioPaths;
269:     }
270: }

Now I have the complete picture. Let me write up the explanation of how denormalized fields are currently calculated.

## The denormalized fields

**Lessons table** (source-level computed, but still denormalized since derived from content):
- `points` — derived from content, not content itself
- `duration` — derived (or manually set for exams)

**Modules table:**
- `total_points` — sum of lesson `points`

**Courses table:**
- `total_duration`, `modules_count`, `lessons_count`, `total_points`

## The derivation rules

**Lesson::recalculatePoints()** (in Lesson model):
- article: `round(str_word_count(strip_tags(article_content)) / 10)`
- quiz/exam: `questions()->count() * 10`
- saves quietly only if changed

**Lesson::recalculateDuration()**:
- exam: skipped entirely (keeps manual time limit)
- article: `max(1, ceil(word_count / 150))` — reading time
- quiz: `max(1, ceil(sum over questions of (question words/150 + audio_duration/60)))`
- saves quietly only if changed

**Module::recalculateStats()**:
- `total_points = lessons()->sum('points')` — one UPDATE, always (no change check)

**Course::recalculateStats()**:
- `modules_count = modules()->count()`
- `lessons_count`, `total_duration`, `total_points` via single aggregate query on lessons (count, sum duration, sum points)
- one UPDATE, always

## Who triggers it (call sites)

Three levels, always triggered imperatively by controllers in DB transactions:

1. **CourseController::update** (metadata save): `$course->recalculateStats()` — nothing lesson-related changed, but stats are refreshed anyway (defensive)
2. **ModuleController::store**: `$course->recalculateStats()` (new empty module: modules_count goes up)
   **ModuleController::destroy**: recalc course
   Module rename/reorder: NO recalc (correct — neither affects stats)
3. **LessonController::store** (new blank article lesson): `recalculateDuration` on lesson + module + course stats
   **LessonController::update** (full content save): after delete-all-questions + re-create + syncQuestions: lesson points + duration, module stats, course stats
   **LessonController::destroy**: module + course stats
   Lesson rename (updateTitle): no recalc (correct)
   Lesson reorder: no recalc (correct)

Module/Course `recalculateStats` always write unconditionally (and touch timestamps — which matters for `CourseController::index`'s `latest('updated_at')` sort! Any lesson edit updates course.updated_at via the course->update() in recalculateStats. That's actually load-bearing: the courses index sorts by updated_at, and lesson saves bump it.)
- Cascade chain is manual: lesson change → recalc lesson → recalc module → recalc course, all within the controller's DB::transaction.
- LessonController::update does full question deletion + recreation (delete-all + re-insert), so points/duration recompute naturally afterwards.
- The update flow loads `$lesson->load('questions')` before recalculate so computeQuizDuration can iterate `$this->questions` (relation cache) — that's why the `load` is there.
- Also note: `Course::recalculateStats` gets lessons via `lessons()` hasMany (both course_id and module_id on lesson — lesson belongs to both; course-level lessons relationship is redundant denormalized relation: lesson has course_id AND module_id).
- Drift risk: writes always go through these controllers so it stays consistent, but there's no event/observer enforcement — any tinker/seed/future code path that writes lessons directly must remember the cascade. Here's the complete picture of how denormalized fields are handled today.

## 1. What's stored where

| Table | Denormalized columns |
|---|---|
| `courses` | `total_duration`, `modules_count`, `lessons_count`, `total_points` |
| `modules` | `total_points` |
| `lessons` | `points`, `duration` (derived from content, not the content itself) |

## 2. The derivation rules (in the models)

**`Lesson::recalculatePoints()`** — derived from content:
- `article` → `round(word_count(strip_tags(article_content)) / 10)`
- `quiz` / `exam` → `questions_count × 10`

**`Lesson::recalculateDuration()`**:
- `exam` → **skipped entirely** — duration is a manually entered time limit
- `article` → `max(1, ceil(words / 150))` (reading time)
- `quiz` → `ceil(Σ(question words / 150 + audio_duration / 60))` — iterates the loaded `questions` relation

**`Module::recalculateStats()`** → `total_points = lessons()->sum('points')`

**`Course::recalculateStats()`** → one aggregate query over `lessons` (`count`, `sum(duration)`, `sum(points)`) + `modules()->count()`

## 3. Who triggers it — an imperative cascade in the controllers

Every write endpoint in the three admin controllers manually chains the recalculation **in order, inside its `DB::transaction`**:

```
lesson change → lesson recalc → module recalc → course recalc
```

| Endpoint | Recalcs performed |
|---|---|
| `LessonController::update` (full content save) | lesson points + duration, module, course |
| `LessonController::store` (new blank lesson) | lesson duration, module, course |
| `LessonController::destroy` | module, course |
| `ModuleController::store` / `destroy` | course |
| `CourseController::update` (metadata only) | course — *defensive; nothing stats-related changed* |
| Renames & reorders | **none** (correct — no stat impact) |

Note `LessonController::update` deletes and recreates **all** questions/answers on every save, then does `$lesson->load('questions')` so `recalculateDuration` can iterate a fresh relation cache — the recompute is forced by the delete-and-reinsert pattern.

## 4. Subtle behaviors worth knowing before a redesign

1. **Write asymmetry.** The Lesson recalc methods only save *if the value changed*, and use `saveQuietly()` (no `updated_at` bump, no events). But `Module::recalculateStats` and `Course::recalculateStats` call `update()` **unconditionally** — always writes, always touches `updated_at`.

2. **That timestamp touch is load-bearing.** `CourseController::index` sorts by `latest('updated_at')`. Because every lesson save cascades to `$course->recalculateStats()`, editing any lesson bubbles the course to the top of the list. A naive redesign that stops touching the course row would silently break that ordering behavior.

3. **No enforcement mechanism.** There are no observers, events, or model hooks. Consistency exists only because all writes funnel through the three admin controllers, each of which remembers the manual cascade. Seeders bypass it entirely: `CourseSeeder`/`LessonSeeder` insert hardcoded, hand-tallied numbers (e.g. course 1: durations `20+45+6+45+30+30+15+35+8 = 234`, points sum `160` — consistent by hand, not by code). `QuestionSeeder`/`AnswerSeeder` likewise.

4. **Double foreign key.** `lessons` carries both `course_id` and `module_id`. Course stats aggregate over `course_id` while module stats aggregate over `module_id` — they only agree because the controller always sets both. Nothing at the schema level guarantees a lesson's `course_id` actually matches its module's `course_id`.

5. **Cost profile.** A lesson save costs ~6 queries for the cascade (plus the delete/recreate of all questions and answers). Cheap at this scale, but the recompute is *total*, not incremental.

---

So in summary: **derived values are denormalized at every level, recomputed via a manually-invoked cascade inside controller transactions, with no event-driven safety net, and hand-maintained seed data.**

What's motivating the redesign — drift concerns, the delete-and-reinsert save flow, wanting observers/events so any write path stays consistent, or something else? That'll shape which direction makes sense (e.g., Eloquent observers vs. computed-on-read accessors vs. query-time aggregation).

## Schema observations relevant to the redesign

1. **Every cascade is `ON DELETE CASCADE`** — deletes propagate automatically at the DB level, but nothing recalculates parent counters on delete at the DB level. The cascade that maintains the † columns is purely the PHP-level controller chain.

2. **`lessons` is double-keyed** — both `course_id` and `module_id` FKs, and nothing guarantees they agree. Course stats aggregate over `course_id`; module stats over `module_id`.

3. **`questions.correct_answer_id` is a circular FK** (questions → answers, while answers → questions). It's added in a separate `Schema::table` step after answers exists, with `nullOnDelete` to survive answer deletion. Correctness of "which answer is right" lives here, not in an `is_correct` flag on answers.

4. **No secondary indexes anywhere** — `order_index`, `course_id`, `module_id`, `lesson_id`, `status` are all unindexed (SQLite doesn't auto-index FK columns). Fine at current scale, but a redesign that moves to query-time aggregation would want them.

5. **All † columns are integers with defaults**, so a "recompute from scratch" path is always possible — every derived value can be rebuilt from the source rows (content, question counts, audio durations).

That last point matters for your redesign: the source-of-truth data (`article_content`, question/answer rows, `audio_duration`, exam `duration`) is all present, so any strategy — event-driven recompute, observers, or dropping the columns and aggregating at read time — is on the table. ## Assistant

_Thinking:_

The user asks how the backend fills the DB — creation order: top-down (course → answers) or bottom-up (answers → course). I already know this from LessonController::syncQuestions and the controllers. Let me answer from what I've read.

Key flows:

**Course creation** (`CourseController::store`): creates a blank draft course only.

**Module creation** (`ModuleController::store`): appends module to course.

**Lesson creation** (`LessonController::store`): creates blank article lesson.

**Full lesson save** (`LessonController::update` → `syncQuestions`): this is the interesting one — it's actually BOTH directions in a sense:

1. Top-down for the shell: course → module → lesson rows are created by separate endpoints at separate times (user creates course, then module, then lesson).
2. But for questions/answers within `syncQuestions`: it's a delete-and-recreate, and the order is **bottom-up-ish with a twist**:
   - Delete ALL existing questions for the lesson (answers cascade-delete via FK)
   - For each question: create question first (without correct_answer_id), then create its answers, then **update the question** to set `correct_answer_id` pointing at the answer
   - So: question → answers → back-patch question. This is why `correct_answer_id` is nullable — the circular FK forces a two-phase write.

So the answer: 
- The hierarchy (course/module/lesson) is created strictly **top-down** across separate HTTP requests as the admin builds the outline.
- Question/answer rows within a lesson save are created **question-first, then answers, then a backfill update** on the question — a hybrid: you can't do pure bottom-up because answers need their question_id, and you can't set correct_answer_id when creating the question because the answer doesn't exist yet. The migration comment even says: "Nullable because answer rows must exist before the pointer can be set."
- Also the stats cascade runs **bottom-up** after content is saved (lesson → module → course).

**Answer: The hierarchy is created strictly top-down. The only bottom-up step is the `correct_answer_id` back-patch.**

Two write paths:

### 1. Runtime (admin controllers) — top-down over multiple requests

The admin builds the tree incrementally over separate HTTP requests, always parent before child:

1. `CourseController::store` — creates a blank draft course (only `status='draft'`, everything else null/default)
2. `ModuleController::store` — appends "New Module" to that course
3. `LessonController::store` — appends "New Lesson" (type=article) to that module
4. `LessonController::update` (the standalone lesson editor save) — fills in the leaf content. Within one transaction:
   - Update the lesson row itself (title, type, article_content / duration)
   - **Delete all existing questions** (answers die automatically via DB cascade)
   - `syncQuestions`: for each incoming question: **create the question row first** (without `correct_answer_id`), **then create its answers** (each needs `question_id`), **then update the question** to point `correct_answer_id` at the chosen answer row.
   
   So question/answer creation is *question-first* (parent-first/top-down within the leaf), with a bottom-up back-patch for the circular correct-answer pointer.

Then the stats cascade runs **bottom-up**: lesson recalc → module recalc → course recalc.

So the runtime answer: **top-down for structure, with one bottom-up back-patch (correct_answer_id) forced by the circular FK, and a bottom-up stats recompute afterwards.**

Why can't it be pure bottom-up? Because `answers.question_id` requires the question to exist. Why can't `correct_answer_id` be set at question creation? Because the answer doesn't exist yet. The nullable column + two-phase write is the escape hatch — the migration comment states this explicitly: "Nullable because answer rows must exist before the pointer can be set."

### 2. Seeders — also top-down

`DatabaseSeeder` calls in order: MajorDepartement → Course → Module → Lesson → Question → Answer. Answers again do the two-phase trick: insert answer, then `Question::whereKey()->update(['correct_answer_id' => ...])` — using a transient `is_correct` flag in the data array.

**Strictly top-down** (course → answers) — with exactly one bottom-up exception, forced by the circular foreign key. There are two write paths:

## 1. Runtime — the admin builds the tree parent-first, across separate requests

```
CourseController::store      → blank draft course (status='draft', everything else null/default)
ModuleController::store      → "New Module" appended to that course
LessonController::store      → "New Lesson" (type=article) appended to that module
LessonController::update     → fills in the leaf: lesson content + questions + answers
```

Each child is created through the parent's relationship (`$course->modules()->create(...)`, `$module->lessons()->create(...)`, `$lesson->questions()->create(...)`) — so the parent row must always exist first. The admin never creates an answer before its question.

## 2. The leaf save (`LessonController::update` → `syncQuestions`) — where it gets interesting

Inside one transaction, per save:

```
1. lesson->update(title, type, article_content / duration)
2. lesson->questions()->delete()          ← ALL existing questions wiped
                                          ← answers die automatically via DB cascade
3. for each incoming question:
     a. question = lesson->questions()->create(...)   ← created WITHOUT correct_answer_id
     b. answers = question->answers()->create(...)    ← each needs question_id
     c. question->update(['correct_answer_id' => answers[chosen]->id])   ← BACK-PATCH
4. then the stats cascade — this part IS bottom-up:
     lesson recalc → module recalc → course recalc
```

So even at the leaf, creation order is **question-first (parent-first)**. The only true bottom-up step is step 3c: pointing `correct_answer_id` *up* from the newly created answer back to the question.

**Why the back-patch exists:** `answers.question_id` requires the question to exist, so answers can't be created first. But `questions.correct_answer_id` requires the answer to exist, so it can't be set when the question is created. The circular FK makes a single-phase write impossible — that's why `correct_answer_id` is nullable, and the migration comment says it outright: *"Nullable because answer rows must exist before the pointer can be set."*

## 3. Seeders — same shape

`DatabaseSeeder` runs in strict top-down order: `MajorDepartement → Course → Module → Lesson → Question → Answer`.

`AnswerSeeder` does the same two-phase trick as the controller: it carries a transient `is_correct` flag in its data array, inserts each answer, then back-patches `Question::whereKey($questionId)->update(['correct_answer_id' => ...])`.

## Two consequences relevant to your redesign

1. **The leaf save is destructive-replace, not diffing.** Every lesson save deletes and recreates *all* questions and answers — even if only one character changed. There's no update-in-place of existing question/answer rows (the frontend sends whole arrays, the backend wipes and rebuilds). This is why audio file handling needs the `keptAudioPaths` / `orphanedPaths` dance, and why the points/duration recompute is always a full recompute.

2. **Row identity is disposable.** Because question/answer IDs are regenerated on every save, nothing can reference them durably yet (e.g., student answer submissions would break if they pointed at answer IDs that get deleted and recreated). If the student-facing side will ever store "which answer did the user pick," this delete-and-recreate pattern is the thing to change first — it interacts directly with how you redesign the recalculation.

So: **structure flows top-down; the correct-answer pointer back-patches bottom-up; stats recompute bottom-up; and leaf content is wholesale replaced rather than updated.**

"Destructive" in the literal SQL sense — let me walk through exactly what happens every time you hit **Save** in the lesson editor:

## What one save actually does

Take a quiz lesson with 5 questions × 4 answers = 20 answer rows in the DB. You fix one typo in question 3 and save. `LessonController::update` does this:

```php
$lesson->update([...]);                    // 1. update the lesson row itself — fine

$lesson->questions()->delete();            // 2. DELETE all 5 question rows
                                           //    → all 20 answer rows die instantly
                                           //      via ON DELETE CASCADE

$keptAudioPaths = $this->syncQuestions(...); // 3. INSERT 5 brand-new question rows
                                           //    + 20 brand-new answer rows
                                           //    + 5 UPDATEs for correct_answer_id
```

`syncQuestions` has no update path at all — it only `$lesson->questions()->create(...)` and `$question->answers()->create(...)`. There is no code that says "this question already exists, update it in place." **Every save of a lesson rebuilds its entire question/answer subtree from scratch.**

## Concretely, the row identities look like this:

| | Before save | After save |
|---|---|---|
| Question 1 | id **1** | id **32** |
| Question 2 | id **2** | id **33** |
| Question 3 (the typo fix) | id **3** | id **34** |
| Question 4 | id **4** | id **35** |
| Question 5 | id **5** | id **36** |
| All 20 answers | ids 1–20 | ids 81–100 (new range) |

Even though you changed one character, all 25 rows are hard-deleted and re-inserted with fresh autoincrement IDs. The old rows are gone — not soft-deleted, not archived.

## The workaround this forces (proof it's a known pain point)

The audio files survive this cycle only through special handling. Since `audio_url` lives on the question row being destroyed, the controller:

1. Snapshots the old questions *before* deleting (`$existingQuestions = $lesson->questions()->get()->keyBy('id')`)
2. Re-attaches the **old** audio path to the **new** question row — but only if the frontend sends back the question's original `id` **and** its `audio_url` (`syncQuestions` lines 236–243)
3. After the transaction, deletes any physical audio files whose paths weren't carried over (`orphanedPaths`)

That's ~30 lines of bookkeeping in the controller that exist *solely* because the rows get destroyed. Same for `storedFilePaths()` on the models. And it's fragile: if the frontend ever drops the `id` from a question in its payload, that question's audio silently loses its DB reference — the file stays on disk but becomes unreachable.

## Why this matters for your redesign

Two reasons this is the thing to look at before (or together with) the denormalized-fields redesign:

1. **Nothing can durably reference a question or answer.** The moment you build the student side — "user picked answer #57 on question #34" — those IDs are landmines: any subsequent edit-save by an admin silently renumbers everything, and the student's submission would point at a deleted row. Similarly `correct_answer_id` churns every save.

2. **It dictates the recalculation design.** The current full-recompute-on-every-save approach "works" precisely because the save path already obliterates and rebuilds everything anyway. If you switch to a proper diff-based sync (update-in-place, upsert, or delete-only-missing), the recalculation strategy needs to be event/observer-driven to catch partial changes — the two changes are coupled.

To be clear on scope: `updateTitle` (renaming from the course outline) is *not* destructive — it's a plain update. Only the full lesson-editor save is. And this is all your own uncommitted F-31 work, so it's very much open to redesign.

Do you want to tackle both together — diff-based question/answer sync + a recalculation strategy that hooks into it — or keep the destructive save for now and redesign only the denormalized counters?

No — courses and modules are updated **in place**. The delete-and-recreate behavior is exclusive to the lesson's question/answer subtree. Here's the full picture:

## Update paths compared

| Endpoint | What it does | Destructive? |
|---|---|---|
| `CourseController::update` | `$course->update($validated)` — one row, in place | ❌ No |
| `ModuleController::update` (rename) | `$module->update(['title' => ...])` | ❌ No |
| `LessonController::updateTitle` (rename) | `$lesson->update(['title' => ...])` | ❌ No |
| `LessonController::update` (full save) | deletes + recreates all questions/answers | ⚠️ **Yes — the only one** |
| Both `reorder` endpoints | mass `update(['order_index' => $index])` per row | ❌ No — in-place |
| All three `destroy` endpoints | cascade delete + file cleanup | Yes, but that's a delete — expected |

So row identity is stable for courses, modules, and lessons themselves — a course keeps its ID from creation until deletion. Only questions and answers are regenerated on every save.

## The one nuance on courses: the cover image

`CourseController::update` is non-destructive for the *row*, but `syncCoverImage` does manage the *file* on disk carefully:

- New image uploaded → old file deleted from the public disk, new one stored, `image_url` updated on the same row
- `remove_image` flag → old file deleted, `image_url` set to null
- Neither → existing path kept as-is

So the course row is stable; only the underlying file gets swapped when you change it. Same *spirit* as the lesson's audio-preservation logic, but much simpler — because there's just one optional file on a single row, not a nested subtree.

## Why the asymmetry exists

It comes down to shape of the data:

- **Course and module own only scalar columns** (title, descriptions, image, status) — the update request is flat, so `$model->update($validated)` just works.
- **The lesson owns a nested collection** — an array of questions, each containing an array of answers, plus per-question audio. Diffing "which of these already exist, which changed, which were removed, and how do answers map to their old rows" is genuinely more logic. The wipe-and-rebuild shortcut avoids all of it at the cost of ID churn.

Which is exactly why I flagged the question/answer sync as the bigger structural decision in your redesign: it's the only place where the backend's write model is "destroy and rebuild" rather than "update in place." If you want the whole tree to behave consistently — stable IDs everywhere, one uniform recalculation story — that's the piece to redesign, and the course/module controllers can stay as they are.

## CourseController — the root, flat CRUD + media

Routes: `GET /dashboard/courses`, `POST /dashboard/courses`, `GET /dashboard/courses/{course}/edit`, `PUT /dashboard/courses/{course}`, `DELETE /dashboard/courses/{course}`

**`index()`** — maps all courses to a flat array for the listing page (title fallback `"Untitled Course"`, image resolved to a URL, denormalized stats passed as `duration`/`modules`/`points`) sorted by `latest('updated_at')`. No pagination — it's a full table map.

**`store()`** — creates a completely blank course: only `status: 'draft'`. Every other column is null/default. Then redirects straight into its editor. (This is the "click New Course → land in the editor" flow.)

**`edit()`** — eager-loads `modules` (ordered by `order_index`, then `id`) and `modules.lessons` (same ordering), then hand-maps the whole tree to arrays for the course editor page. Note it maps the *denormalized* stats (`total_duration`, `modules_count`, …) — it never recomputes them; it trusts the stored values.

**`update($request, $course)`** — the metadata save:
```php
$validated = $request->safe()->except(['image', 'remove_image']);
$validated['image_url'] = $this->syncCoverImage($request, $course);
$course->update($validated);          // in-place row update
$course->recalculateStats();          // defensive — nothing stat-related changed
redirect → courses list
```
`syncCoverImage()` (private): new upload → delete old file, store new, return new path; `remove_image` flag → delete old file, return null; otherwise → keep the existing path untouched. File operations happen *outside* any transaction here — a failed save could delete an old image before the DB write fails. (In practice `update()` after a successful store rarely fails, but it's a small race.)

**`destroy($course)`** — collects `storedFilePaths()` **before** deleting (cover image + all nested question audio), deletes the row in a transaction (modules/lessons/questions/answers die via DB cascade), then deletes the files from disk **after** commit.

**`resolveMediaUrl()`** (static) — shared helper: passes through `http(s)://` URLs, otherwise converts a public-disk path to a full URL. LessonController reuses it for audio.

---

## ModuleController — the middle tier, outline operations only

Routes (all inside `scopeBindings()`): `POST .../courses/{course}/modules`, `PATCH .../modules/reorder`, `PATCH .../modules/{module}`, `DELETE .../modules/{module}`

**`store()`** — appends `"New Module"` with `order_index = max + 1` inside a transaction, then `$course->recalculateStats()` (bumps `modules_count`). Redirects `back()`.

**`update()`** — renames only. Validates `title`, updates, done. No recalc, no transaction (single write).

**`reorder()`** — validates the incoming `module_ids` array: must exist, be distinct, and *belong to this course* (`Rule::exists('modules')->where('course_id', ...)`). Then in a transaction, one `UPDATE` per row setting `order_index` to array position. No stats recalc (order doesn't affect stats).

**`destroy()`** — collects the module's audio paths first, deletes the module in a transaction (lessons + everything below cascade), **reindexes remaining siblings** (`order_index = 0,1,2...` only where changed), recalcs course stats, then deletes orphaned audio files after commit.

---

## LessonController — the heavy one: leaf content + the destructive sync

Routes (inside `scopeBindings()`): `POST .../modules/{module}/lessons`, `PATCH .../lessons/reorder`, `GET .../lessons/{lesson}/edit`, `PATCH .../lessons/{lesson}/title`, `PUT .../lessons/{lesson}`, `DELETE .../lessons/{lesson}`

**`store()`** — appends a blank `"New Lesson"` (`type: article`, next `order_index`) inside a transaction, then `recalculateDuration()` on the lesson (a blank article computes to duration 1), plus module and course recalcs. Redirects `back()` — the frontend then opens the standalone lesson editor.

**`edit()`** — renders `Dashboard/Lessons/Editor` with the lesson's full subtree: questions ordered, each question's `correct_answer_index` recovered by searching its answers for `correct_answer_id`, audio URL resolved, `audio_file: null` (only a DB-backed path is sent — new uploads happen client-side).

**`updateTitle()`** — rename from the course outline without content. Plain update, no recalc.

**`reorder()`** — same pattern as modules: validated id list scoped to the module, transactional per-row `order_index` writes.

**`update()`** — the full lesson-editor save, the most involved endpoint:
```
before transaction:  $previousAudioPaths   (current paths on disk)
                     $existingQuestions    (current rows, keyed by id)

transaction:
    lesson->update(title, type, article_content | duration)
    lesson->questions()->delete()           ← subtree wiped
    if type !== 'article':
        $keptAudioPaths = syncQuestions()   ← recreate everything
    lesson->load('questions')               ← refresh relation cache
    lesson->recalculatePoints()             ← words/10 or questions×10
    lesson->recalculateDuration()           ← reading/audio math (exam skipped)
    module->recalculateStats()              ← sum(lesson points)
    course->recalculateStats()              ← aggregates + bumps updated_at

after commit:  delete files in array_diff($previousAudioPaths, $keptAudioPaths)
redirect → course editor
```

**`syncQuestions()`** (private) — for each incoming question, in array order: resolve audio (new `UploadedFile` → store to `lessons/audio`; else re-attach the old row's path if the payload carried the old `id` + `audio_url`), create the question, create its answers, back-patch `correct_answer_id`.

**`destroy()`** — collect audio paths, delete in a transaction, reindex sibling lessons, recalc module + course, delete files after commit, `back()`.

---

## Shared patterns across all three

1. **Transaction discipline** — multi-row writes always wrapped; single-row writes (`update`, `updateTitle`) aren't.
2. **Files are only touched after commit** — paths always collected *before* the transaction, disk deletion *after*. So a rollback never leaves orphaned deletes (except the `syncCoverImage` nuance in CourseController::update noted above).
3. **`back()` vs explicit redirects** — outline operations return `back()` (stay on the course editor); the two "finished editing" saves redirect (course → list, lesson → course editor).
4. **The recalc cascade lives in the controllers, not the models** — each endpoint hand-codes which level(s) to refresh. `scopeBindings()` guarantees the route chain `course → module → lesson` via each child's immediate parent FK (`module_id`) — but the lesson's `course_id` column is *not* verified by routing; the controllers keep it in sync by passing `$course->id` explicitly at creation.
5. **Validation split** — flat metadata saves use form requests (`CourseUpdateRequest`, `LessonUpdateRequest`); quick inline operations (`updateTitle`, `reorder`) use inline `$request->validate()`.

So the architecture is: **Course and Module controllers are thin, in-place, outline-level CRUD; LessonController is where all the complexity concentrates** — subtree rebuild, media retention, and the bottom-up recalc cascade. Any redesign of the denormalized fields mostly concerns itself with that last controller.

The reorder algorithm:

Backend (ModuleController::reorder):
```php
public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course): RedirectResponse
{
    $validated = $request->validate([
        'module_ids' => ['required', 'array', 'min:1'],
        'module_ids.*' => [
            'required',
            'integer',
            'distinct',
            Rule::exists('modules', 'id')->where('course_id', $course->id),
        ],
    ]);

    DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $validated): void {
        foreach ($validated['module_ids'] as $index => $moduleId) {
            Module::query()
                ->where('course_id', $course->id)
                ->whereKey($moduleId)
                ->update(['order_index' => $index]);
        }
    });

    return back();
}
```

How it works:
- Frontend sends the FULL ordered list of module ids after the drag (array position = new order)
- Validation: required, non-empty array, each id must be integer, distinct (no duplicates), and must exist in modules table belonging to this course (scoped exists rule)
- Inside a transaction: for each id, one UPDATE setting order_index = its array position (0-based)
- Returns back() — Inertia re-renders with fresh server state

Key characteristics:
- Position-based (0..n-1), not gap-based (no 10, 20, 30 spacing)
- One UPDATE query per item — N queries for N modules (could be a single CASE WHEN or upsert, but N is small)
- Must send the complete list — partial lists only reorder the sent subset; items not included keep their old order_index (could collide with new ones → ties broken by id in the sort)
- It does NOT validate that the list is a permutation of ALL modules in the course — a subset is allowed. Ties are possible if you send a subset (e.g., send [3,5] when there are 5 modules: modules 3 and 5 get index 0 and 1, while module 1,2,4 keep old indexes 0,1,2 → duplicates → sort is by order_index then id... the read side sorts orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id'))
- The transaction protects atomicity but each update is independent; concurrent reorders could interleave (last write wins per row)

### Reordering algorithm

Important clarification: CourseController has no reorder — courses are ordered by updated_at on the index. Reorder exists for modules (ModuleController::reorder) and lessons (LessonController::reorder).

The algorithm, step by step:

**Frontend (CourseContent.jsx):**
1. dnd-kit `DndContext` + `SortableContext` with `verticalListSortingStrategy`, PointerSensor with 4px activation constraint (so clicks don't trigger drags)
2. On drag end (`handleModuleDragEnd` / `handleLessonDragEnd`):
   - Guard: no target or same position → no-op
   - Find from/to indexes by matching active.id/over.id
   - `arrayMove(items, from, to)` — dnd-kit's immutable splice — computes the new array
   - **Optimistic update**: `setOrderedModules(reordered)` / `setOrderedLessons(reordered)` — UI updates instantly
   - Persist: `router.patch` to the reorder route with `{ module_ids: reordered.map(m => m.id) }` — the FULL ordered id list (array position = new order), with `preserveScroll: true`, `showProgress: false`, `only: ['course']` (partial reload — only refreshes the course prop, doesn't re-render the whole page)
3. Local state also syncs from server props via useEffect when `modules`/`moduleItem.lessons` change

**Backend (ModuleController::reorder, LessonController::reorder — same shape):**
1. Validate: `module_ids` required, array, min:1, each `required|integer|distinct`, and `Rule::exists('modules', 'id')->where('course_id', $course->id)` — every id must belong to this course (authorization/scope guard against cross-course ids)
2. In a DB transaction: for each id at array position `$index`: one `UPDATE modules SET order_index = $index WHERE course_id = ? AND id = ?`
3. `back()` — Inertia returns fresh page props (re-render with canonical order)

**Key characteristics:**
- **Position-based, dense, 0-based**: order_index = 0,1,2,...N-1. No gaps (not fractional/gap-based like 10,20,30)
- **Full-list semantics**: the client sends the complete permutation; the array index becomes the new order_index. It's not "move item X to position Y" — it's "here is the entire new order"
- **N UPDATE queries** for N items (one per row) inside a transaction — fine for small N; a single CASE-based UPDATE or `upsert` could do it in one query but isn't warranted at this scale
- **Subset is not rejected**: validation doesn't check the list is a *complete* permutation of the course's modules. Sending a partial list renumbers only those rows; the rest keep old indexes → duplicate order_index values possible → read side breaks ties with `orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id')`. (Only reachable via a hand-crafted request, since the UI always sends the full list.)
- **Insertion appends at max+1**: `store()` computes `max(order_index) + 1`, so new items go last
- **Deletion reindexes densely**: `destroy()` renumbers remaining siblings 0..n-1 to repair the gap
- **No recalc**: reorder doesn't trigger stats recalculation (order doesn't affect points/duration)
- **Optimistic UI with server reconciliation**: the patch uses `only: ['course']` so the server response refreshes just the course prop, and the useEffect syncs canonical state back — if the server rejects (validation error), Inertia shows errors but the local optimistic order stays until props reload... actually on error, no course prop refresh — optimistic state might diverge. Edge case worth mentioning: no onError handler, so a failed reorder leaves the optimistic local order in place. Minor.
- Concurrency: two simultaneous reorders → last write wins per row; transaction gives atomicity but not conflict detection (no versioning)

Read side: `CourseController::edit` eager loads with `orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id')` — id as tiebreaker.

Also lesson reorder is scoped within a module; module drag is disabled while editing titles (`dragDisabled`).

## CourseController

```php
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers\Admin;

use App\Http\Controllers\Controller;
use App\Http\Requests\Admin\CourseUpdateRequest;
use App\Models\Course;
use App\Models\Lesson;
use App\Models\Module;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Storage;
use Inertia\Inertia;
use Inertia\Response;

class CourseController extends Controller
{
    /**
     * Display the courses management directory.
     */
    public function index(): Response
    {
        $courses = Course::query()
            ->latest('updated_at')
            ->get()
            ->map(fn (Course $course): array => [
                'id' => $course->id,
                'title' => $course->title ?: 'Untitled Course',
                'category' => $course->category,
                'description' => $course->short_description ?? '',
                'image_url' => self::resolveMediaUrl($course->image_url),
                'status' => $course->status,
                'duration' => $course->total_duration,
                'modules' => $course->modules_count,
                'points' => $course->total_points,
            ])
            ->values();

        return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses', [
            'courses' => $courses,
        ]);
    }

    /**
     * Create a blank draft course and redirect to its editor.
     */
    public function store(): RedirectResponse
    {
        $course = Course::create([
            'status' => 'draft',
        ]);

        return redirect()->route('dashboard.courses.edit', $course);
    }

    /**
     * Display the course editor hydrated from the persisted course tree.
     */
    public function edit(Course $course): Response
    {
        $course->load([
            'modules' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id'),
            'modules.lessons' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id'),
        ]);

        return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses/Editor', [
            'course' => [
                'id' => $course->id,
                'title' => $course->title ?? '',
                'category' => $course->category ?? '',
                'short_description' => $course->short_description ?? '',
                'long_description' => $course->long_description ?? '',
                'image_url' => self::resolveMediaUrl($course->image_url),
                'status' => $course->status,
                'total_duration' => $course->total_duration,
                'modules_count' => $course->modules_count,
                'lessons_count' => $course->lessons_count,
                'total_points' => $course->total_points,
                'modules' => $course->modules->map(fn (Module $module): array => [
                    'id' => $module->id,
                    'title' => $module->title,
                    'lessons' => $module->lessons->map(fn (Lesson $lesson): array => [
                        'id' => $lesson->id,
                        'title' => $lesson->title,
                        'type' => $lesson->type,
                    ])->values()->all(),
                ])->values()->all(),
            ],
        ]);
    }

    /**
     * Validate and save course metadata as draft or published.
     */
    public function update(CourseUpdateRequest $request, Course $course): RedirectResponse
    {
        $validated = $request->safe()->except(['image', 'remove_image']);
        $validated['image_url'] = $this->syncCoverImage($request, $course);

        $course->update($validated);
        $course->recalculateStats();

        return redirect()->route('dashboard.courses');
    }

    /**
     * Delete a course and clean up all stored media files.
     */
    public function destroy(Course $course): RedirectResponse
    {
        $storedPaths = $course->storedFilePaths();

        DB::transaction(function () use ($course): void {
            $course->delete();
        });

        if ($storedPaths !== []) {
            Storage::disk('public')->delete($storedPaths);
        }

        return redirect()->route('dashboard.courses');
    }

    /**
     * Handle cover image replacement or removal on the public disk.
     */
    private function syncCoverImage(Request $request, Course $course): ?string
    {
        if ($request->hasFile('image')) {
            if ($course->image_url && str_starts_with($course->image_url, 'courses/')) {
                Storage::disk('public')->delete($course->image_url);
            }

            return $request->file('image')->store('courses', 'public');
        }

        if ($request->boolean('remove_image')) {
            if ($course->image_url && str_starts_with($course->image_url, 'courses/')) {
                Storage::disk('public')->delete($course->image_url);
            }

            return null;
        }

        return $course->image_url;
    }

    /**
     * Resolve a relative public-disk path or pass through external URLs.
     */
    public static function resolveMediaUrl(?string $path): ?string
    {
        if (! $path) {
            return null;
        }

        if (str_starts_with($path, 'http://') || str_starts_with($path, 'https://')) {
            return $path;
        }

        return Storage::disk('public')->url($path);
    }
}
```

## How reordering currently works

There are two reorder endpoints — `ModuleController::reorder` and `LessonController::reorder` — and they're identical in shape. The lesson one (renamed for space):

```php
public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course, Module $module): RedirectResponse
{
    $validated = $request->validate([
        'lesson_ids' => ['required', 'array', 'min:1'],
        'lesson_ids.*' => [
            'required',
            'integer',
            'distinct',
            Rule::exists('lessons', 'id')->where('module_id', $module->id),
        ],
    ]);

    DB::transaction(function () use ($module, $validated): void {
        foreach ($validated['lesson_ids'] as $index => $lessonId) {
            Lesson::query()
                ->where('module_id', $module->id)
                ->whereKey($lessonId)
                ->update(['order_index' => $index]);
        }
    });

    return back();
}
```

**The algorithm in one sentence:** the client sends the *complete* id list in its new order; the array position becomes the new `order_index`.

**Frontend side** (`CourseContent.jsx`, both module and lesson variants):

```js
const handleModuleDragEnd = ({ active, over }) => {
    if (!over || active.id === over.id) return;          // 1. no-op guards

    const from = orderedModules.findIndex(/* ... */);
    const to = orderedModules.findIndex(/* ... */);

    const reordered = arrayMove(orderedModules, from, to); // 2. dnd-kit splice
    setOrderedModules(reordered);                          // 3. OPTIMISTIC update

    router.patch(
        route('dashboard.courses.modules.reorder', courseId),
        { module_ids: reordered.map((mod) => mod.id) },    // 4. full id list
        { preserveScroll: true, showProgress: false, only: ['course'] },
    );
};
```

Step by step:

1. **Drag mechanics** — dnd-kit `DndContext` + `SortableContext` (vertical strategy), `PointerSensor` with a 4px activation distance so clicks (rename, accordion toggle) don't start drags. Module dragging is additionally disabled while a title input is open.
2. **Reorder computation** — `arrayMove(items, from, to)` is a pure splice: removes the dragged item and reinserts it at the target index. No fractional/gap logic, no persistence at this point.
3. **Optimistic render** — local state updates instantly, so the UI reorders before the server confirms. A `useEffect` syncs local state back whenever the server's `course` prop changes.
4. **Persistence** — `router.patch` sends the full id array. `only: ['course']` does a *partial reload*: the server re-renders just the `course` prop, which is the canonical order coming back from `edit()`'s `orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id')` eager loads.

**Design properties worth knowing:**

| Property | Current behavior |
|---|---|
| Numbering scheme | **Dense, 0-based positions** — `0, 1, 2, … N-1`. No gaps, no "insert between" fractions. |
| Payload semantics | **Full-list replacement**, not "move X to position Y" |
| Write cost | One `UPDATE` per item, N queries for N items, inside a transaction (a single `CASE`-based update could do it in 1 query, unwarranted at this scale) |
| Validation | ids must be integers, **distinct**, and **exist within the parent** (`Rule::exists` scoped by `course_id` / `module_id`) — this doubles as a cross-course tamper guard |
| Subset requests | **Not rejected** — a partial list renumbers only those rows, leaving stale duplicates in `order_index`. Read-side tiebreaker is `orderBy('id')`. Only reachable via a hand-crafted request; the UI always sends the full list. |
| New items | `store()` appends at `max(order_index) + 1` |
| Deleted items | `destroy()` renumbers survivors `0..n-1` to keep the sequence dense |
| Stats | **No recalculation** — order doesn't affect points/duration, so reorder endpoints skip the cascade entirely |
| Failure handling | The frontend has **no `onError`** on the reorder patch — if validation fails, the optimistic local order stays diverged until the next full page load |
| Concurrency | Last write wins per row; the transaction gives atomicity but no conflict detection |

That's the whole mechanism — deliberately simple: dense positional indexes, full-permutation payloads, optimistic UI, partial-reload reconciliation. For your redesign, the reorder endpoints are actually the *cleanest* behaved writes in the system (scoped, validated, transactional, no stats coupling) — they'd barely change. The interesting questions are all in `update`/`destroy` and the recalc cascade.
