# The `index` Method — Explained Simply

## The big picture first

Think of this method as a **librarian preparing a display shelf**.

The database is a storage room full of course folders. The librarian (this method) doesn't bring the whole room to the visitor — she:

1. Walks into the room and grabs **all the course folders**
2. Puts them in order — **most recently touched first**
3. For each folder, writes a **small index card**: just the title, a photo reference, and the summary numbers written on the folder's cover
4. Hands the stack of cards to the receptionist (the React page), who displays them

The visitor never sees the folders themselves — only the cards. Let's go through each step.

---

## Line 1: The method signature

```php
public function index(): Response
```

Read it in plain English: *"Everyone can call a function named `index`, and it promises to hand back a Response."*

- **`public`** — any code is allowed to call this. Laravel specifically needs it public, because *it* is the one calling it. When a visitor opens `/dashboard/courses` in their browser, Laravel's routing system looks up "which method handles this?" and finds `index`. You never see Laravel call it — it just happens.
- **`index`** — a convention name meaning "show me the list." In Laravel, `index` = list everything, `show` = show one, `store` = save a new one, and so on. Any Laravel developer opening this file instantly knows what `index` does before reading a line.
- **`: Response`** — a *promise about what comes back*. This says "I will return an Inertia Response object" (the thing that eventually becomes a web page). If you accidentally wrote `return 'hello';` (returning plain text), PHP would refuse and error out — the promise acts as a safety net.

---

## Line 2: Starting the database question

```php
$courses = Course::query()
```

`Course` is the **model** — the PHP class that represents the `courses` database table. Think of the model as *the official translator between PHP and the table*: "the table has a row? I'll turn it into a PHP object. You want to save an object? I'll write it back as a row."

`::query()` means: *"Start preparing a question for the database — but don't ask it yet."*

This is the important subtlety: **nothing has touched the database at this point.** You've just picked up a blank questionnaire. The next lines will fill in that questionnaire ("...sorted like this", "...filtered like that"), and only later does someone actually submit it.

Why write `Course::query()` instead of just `Course::latest(...)`? Purely style — both work. The explicit form makes it obvious a query is being built, and reads top-to-bottom nicely.

---

## Line 3: The sort order

```php
    ->latest('updated_at')
```

This adds one instruction to the questionnaire: *"Sort by the `updated_at` column, newest first."*

Every table in this app automatically has two timestamp columns that Laravel maintains for free:

- `created_at` — the moment the row was born
- `updated_at` — the moment the row was **last changed** (Laravel updates it automatically on every save)

`latest('updated_at')` is just a friendlier spelling of "order by `updated_at` descending." The result: the course the admin touched most recently appears at the **top** of the list, and stale untouched courses sink to the bottom.

**The hidden dependency (worth remembering for your redesign):** "last touched" here means "last time the course *row itself* was written to." And remember — every time anyone edits a lesson or module inside the course, the recalculation cascade rewrites the course row (to update its summary numbers), which refreshes `updated_at` as a side effect. So this sort actually means "courses with recent activity inside them float to the top." If your redesign stops rewriting the course row on every internal edit, **this sorting behavior silently changes** — courses would stop bubbling up when you edit their lessons.

---

## Line 4: Actually asking the database

```php
    ->get()
```

This is the moment the questionnaire gets submitted. `get()` says: *"Okay, run it — go to the database, fetch every matching row, and bring them back."*

What comes back is a **Collection**: a PHP object that's basically a supercharged array, with handy methods (`map`, `filter`, `sum`, ...) attached. Inside it: one `Course` object per row in the table. Ten courses in the database → ten `Course` objects in the collection.

At this point we have *everything* — every column of every course. That's more than the page needs, which is what the next step fixes.

---

## Line 5: The transformation — `map`

```php
    ->map(fn (Course $course): array => [
```

`map` means: *"Take each item in the collection, transform it into something else, and collect the results into a new collection."* Like an assembly line: raw folder goes in one side, index card comes out the other. The original folders are untouched.

`fn (Course $course): array => [...]` is a **short anonymous function** (an "arrow function"). In longhand it would be:

```php
->map(function (Course $course) {
    return [
        // the card's fields...
    ];
});
```

The arrow version is just terser. It says: *"For each course, return this array."*

Two things happen in this transformation, and they're the real reason `map` exists here:

1. **Whitelisting.** The database row has ~13 columns. The page needs 9. By building a fresh array by hand, the method *decides exactly what the frontend is allowed to see*. Nothing sneaks through — if someone later adds a sensitive column to the table, it won't leak to the browser until someone deliberately adds it here.
2. **Renaming for the frontend.** The page receives friendlier names: the column `modules_count` becomes just `modules`, `total_duration` becomes `duration`, `short_description` becomes `description`. The React page never has to know the database's naming.

---

## Lines 6–14: The index card itself, field by field

```php
'id' => $course->id,
```
The row's ID number — its permanent identity. The frontend uses it to build links like "edit course 5" and to know which course to delete. IDs never change, which makes them the safe thing to build URLs around.

```php
'title' => $course->title ?: 'Untitled Course',
```
The title — **with a fallback**. Look closely at the operator: `?:` (not `??`).

- `?:` means: *"use the left side if it's truthy; otherwise the right side."* In PHP, "truthy" excludes not just `null` but also **empty string**, `0`, and so on.
- So this handles **two** bad cases: a course with no title at all (`null`) *and* a course whose title is an empty string `""`.

Why does that matter? Remember `store()`: clicking "New Course" creates a row with **only** `status: 'draft'` — the title is `null`. Without this fallback, the list would show a blank card. With it, you see the friendly placeholder *"Untitled Course"*.

```php
'category' => $course->category,
```
Passed through completely raw — `null` stays `null`. The frontend is trusted to display nothing (or a placeholder) when it's missing. Deliberately *no* fallback here, unlike title.

```php
'description' => $course->short_description ?? '',
```
The short blurb — with a *different kind* of fallback. `??` (null coalescing) only kicks in for `null`, **not** for empty string. So:

- `null` → becomes `''` (empty string)
- `''` → stays `''`

Compare with the title line and you'll spot the inconsistency: `?:` catches both `null` and `""`, while `??` catches only `null`. In practice the outcome is nearly identical (both end up displaying nothing), but it's a subtle style wobble in the same function — the kind of thing a cleanup pass could normalize.

```php
'image_url' => self::resolveMediaUrl($course->image_url),
```
The cover photo — but *transformed*, not passed through. This calls the helper method defined at the bottom of the same class (`self::` = "call it on my own class"). What the helper does, in plain terms:

- The database stores a **relative path** like `courses/abc123.jpg` (where the file lives on the server's disk).
- But a browser can't display a relative path — it needs a **full URL** like `https://yourapp.com/storage/courses/abc123.jpg`.
- The helper does that conversion. If the stored value is already a full `http...` URL, it passes it through untouched. If it's `null` (no photo), it returns `null`.

So the frontend always receives something directly usable.

```php
'status' => $course->status,
```
Either `'draft'` or `'published'` — the database column itself enforces this with a check constraint, so no validation needed here. The page uses it to show the little status badge.

```php
'duration' => $course->total_duration,
'modules'  => $course->modules_count,
'points'   => $course->total_points,
```
The three **summary numbers** — and these are the most conceptually important lines in the method for your redesign.

Here's the key idea. The app could compute these numbers on the spot: *"open every module of this course, count them; open every lesson, add up durations and points..."* That would mean walking the whole course tree **every single time the list page loads**. Instead, the app does what a student does with a textbook summary on the cover: **the numbers are pre-computed and written onto the course row itself** (`total_duration`, `modules_count`, `total_points` are ordinary columns in the `courses` table). Whenever a lesson changes, the recalculation cascade re-adds everything up and rewrites these three numbers.

So in `index`, these lines are just **reading three numbers off the cover** — instant, one query, zero math. The *cost* of that speed is the thing you already know: the numbers are only correct if every write path remembers to recalculate. **This method blindly trusts them.** If a bug ever skips a recalculation, this page will confidently display wrong numbers and nothing will complain.

---

## Line 15: Renumbering the stack

```php
    ->values();
```

A small piece of defensive housekeeping. Collections (like PHP arrays) keep track of their keys. After `map`, keys are `0, 1, 2, ...` — perfectly sequential. `values()` says *"throw away whatever keys exist and renumber from zero."*

Right now it changes nothing. So why is it there? Because of how JSON works:

- Sequential keys `0,1,2` → JSON **array** → `[...]` → JavaScript `.map()` works ✓
- Non-sequential keys (say `5, 9, 12`, which can happen after certain collection operations) → JSON **object** → `{"5": ..., "9": ...}` → JavaScript `.map()` **crashes**, because objects don't have `.map()`

So `values()` is insurance: no matter what collection operations someone adds above it in the future, the thing handed to the frontend is *guaranteed* to serialize as a clean array. It's the kind of line that looks useless until the day it saves you.

---

## Lines 17–20: Handing the cards to the receptionist

```php
return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses', [
    'courses' => $courses,
]);
```

This is where PHP-land ends and the browser begins.

`Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses', ...)` tells Laravel: *"Render the React page component that lives at `resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Courses/index.jsx`."* Inertia finds that file by the name — the string `'Dashboard/Courses'` maps directly to the folder path.

The second argument is the **props** — the data package handed to that React component:

```jsx
// resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Courses/index.jsx receives:
export default function Index({ courses }) {
    // courses = the array of index cards we just built
```

The magic of Inertia is *how* this reaches the browser:

- **First visit** (typed URL, refresh): Laravel returns a full HTML page with the props embedded in it — the React app renders on the server first, so the page appears complete.
- **Inertia navigation** (clicked a link inside the app): no HTML comes back — just the props as JSON, and React swaps the page in place. Much faster, feels like a native app.

Either way, the React component ends up holding exactly the array of cards this method built — nothing more, nothing less.

---

## The whole thing in one breath

> *"Fetch every course, newest-touched first; for each one write a small card with a safe title, a usable image URL, and the pre-computed summary numbers; guarantee the result is a proper array; hand the stack to the Courses page."*

And the one design fact to carry into your redesign: **this method is a pure consumer of the denormalized numbers.** It does zero math and zero verification. Its correctness is 100% inherited from the write paths. That's why any redesign of the recalculation system ripples straight into what this page displays — and also why, if you ever switch to computing numbers at read time, this method is where the change would land (the `map` fields would read live-aggregated values instead of stored columns).

## 1. What if I use `Course::latest` instead of `Course::query()->latest`?

**Nothing changes.** They're identical — `Course::latest()` is just the short form.

Here's why. In Laravel, every model has a magic `__callStatic`. When you write `Course::latest('updated_at')`, PHP sees "there's no static `latest` method on Course" and forwards it to a fresh query builder: `Course::query()->latest('updated_at')`. Literally the same object, same SQL:

```php
Course::latest('updated_at')      // sugar — forwarded via __callStatic
Course::query()->latest('updated_at')  // explicit
```

The explicit `::query()` form is a mild style preference, not a correctness thing. Two small arguments people cite for it:

- **Discoverability** — `Course::query()` signals "a query is being built" before you chain `.where()`, `.get()`, etc.
- **Static-analysis friendliness** — IDEs/PHPStan infer types slightly more reliably on the explicit form.

But functionally? `Course::latest()` is 100% equivalent. Use whichever reads better to you.

---

## 2. Why use `map` at all?

Because raw model rows are a **bad API contract**. `map` is where the raw row gets shaped into exactly what the page needs — nothing more, nothing less.

Look at what each side would be without it:

```php
// WITHOUT map — you'd have to return the raw collection
return $courses;  // every column, every row, serialized wholesale
```

The frontend would receive objects bloated with fields it doesn't use (`created_at`, `updated_at`, `image_url` internals, future internal-only columns...). Worse, three *invisible* problems appear:

**Problem 1 — Model serialization quirks.** Eloquent models don't serialize like plain arrays. `map`-ing to plain arrays gives you clean, predictable JSON with zero surprises.

**Problem 2 — The frontend gets coupled to the database.** If the React page reads `$course->short_description` directly, then renaming that column later (or moving it to a related table) breaks the frontend. With `map`, the database can change freely — you just update the map body and the prop names stay stable.

**Problem 3 — No gatekeeping.** Nothing stops internal-only or sensitive-ish fields from reaching the browser. `map` is the checkpoint that says "this is ALL the frontend gets."

With `map`, the contract is explicit: the page receives exactly these 9 keys and nothing else. It's the boundary where database-land ends and frontend-land begins.

---

## 3. Add a fallback for the description

Yes — worth doing for consistency. Note the current line already handles `null` via `??`:

```php
'description' => $course->short_description ?? '',
```

The `??` only catches `null`, so an empty string `''` stays `''`. The `title` line above it uses `?:`, which catches both `null` *and* `''`. To match that behavior:

**Change:**
```php
'description' => $course->short_description ?: 'No description yet.',
```

Or, if you'd rather show nothing than filler text, keep it minimal but consistent:
```php
'description' => $course->short_description ?: '',
```

The first version is friendlier for the card UI (an empty paragraph looks like a rendering bug); the second is more neutral. Either way, switching `??` → `?:` makes description behave like title.

---

## 4. Is `resolveMediaUrl` even necessary? Can't it be passed directly?

**Great instinct to question it** — and in this codebase, no, the helper is *not* strictly necessary *today*. Here's the honest breakdown:

**What the helper does right now:**
- `null` → `null` (skip)
- `http(s)://...` → pass through unchanged (external URLs)
- otherwise → prefix with the public-disk base URL

**Could you skip it?** Only if every stored `image_url` were guaranteed to be a bare relative path and never `null`. But:

1. **`null` is common** — `store()` creates courses with no image, and the column is nullable. Without the guard, the frontend gets `null` anyway, so the helper's null branch is redundant *here*.
2. **The `http://` passthrough matters** — if anyone ever pastes an external image URL (e.g., a CDN link) instead of uploading, the helper won't wrongly prefix it with your local `/storage/` base. That's a real correctness case, not paranoia.

**Where it earns its keep architecturally:** the *same* helper is reused in `edit()` and `LessonController` for audio. If you inline the logic, you duplicate the `http://` passthrough logic in 3+ places. The helper is the single point of truth for "how does a stored path become a browser-usable URL."

**Verdict:** keep it. It's 10 lines, used in 3 places, and the `http://` passthrough is a real case. Inlining saves nothing and couples every call site to the storage-disk detail.

---

## 5. Add fallbacks for duration, modules, and points

Same pattern as the description — these columns are `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, so they're never `null` in practice. The `??`/`?:` fallbacks would be purely defensive. Still reasonable to add for consistency:

```php
'duration' => $course->total_duration ?? 0,
'modules'  => $course->modules_count ?? 0,
'points'   => $course->total_points ?? 0,
```

But note: unlike `title`/`description` (nullable columns where fallbacks are *load-bearing*), these three are `NOT NULL` — so the fallbacks here are cosmetic insurance, not behavior. The real question is whether you want the controller to normalize aggressively (frontend never sees `null`) or trust the schema. Both defensible; current code trusts the schema.

---

## Putting it all together — the revised `index`

If you want to apply 3, 4, and 5, here's the full method with all changes:

```php
public function index(): Response
{
    $courses = Course::query()
        ->latest('updated_at')
        ->get()
        ->map(fn (Course $course): array => [
            'id' => $course->id,
            'title' => $course->title ?: 'Untitled Course',
            'category' => $course->category,
            'description' => $course->short_description ?: '',
            'image_url' => self::resolveMediaUrl($course->image_url),
            'status' => $course->status,
            'duration' => $course->total_duration ?? 0,
            'modules' => $course->modules_count ?? 0,
            'points' => $course->total_points ?? 0,
        ])
        ->values();

    return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses', [
        'courses' => $courses,
    ]);
}
```

Changes from current code:
- Line `description`: `??` → `?:` (matches title's falsy handling)
- Lines `duration`/`modules`/`points`: added `?? 0` (defensive normalization)

**Unchanged:** `Course::query()` (keep or swap for `Course::latest()` — identical), `map` (the API contract), `resolveMediaUrl` (keep — reused in 3 places, handles the external-URL case).

public static function resolveMediaUrl(?string $path): ?string

}

## What the inline version deliberately drops

The helper had a third branch — the `http://`/`https://` passthrough. The inline version omits it, and that's safe because:

- `courses.image_url` is **only ever written** by `syncCoverImage()` → `$request->file('image')->store('courses', 'public')` — always a relative path like `courses/abc.jpg`, or `null`
- `questions.audio_url` is **only ever written** by `syncQuestions()` → `->store('lessons/audio', 'public')` — same deal

Neither column can hold an external URL in this system, so the passthrough branch is dead code. The trade-off: if "paste an external image URL" ever becomes a feature, this ternary would mangle it — the guard would need to return at that point.

**Why not a model accessor instead?** (Laravel's "native" way to kill such helpers — an `Attribute::get` on `image_url` that auto-resolves everywhere.) Because it would silently break `syncCoverImage()` and the audio-cleanup code, which read the **raw path** to delete files — they'd receive full URLs and `Storage::delete()` would delete nothing. Doing accessors properly requires splitting raw-path vs. URL attributes — a bigger refactor than you asked for. The inline ternary is the honest minimal version.

## Backend — `CourseController.php`

**`index()`** — keys now match the schema exactly:

```php
public function index(): Response
{
    $courses = Course::latest('updated_at')
        ->get()
        ->map(fn (Course $course): array => [
            'id' => $course->id,
            'title' => $course->title ?: 'Untitled Course',
            'category' => $course->category,
            'short_description' => $course->short_description ?: '',
            'image_url' => $course->image_url
                ? Storage::disk('public')->url($course->image_url)
                : null,
            'status' => $course->status,
            'total_duration' => $course->total_duration ?? 0,
            'modules_count' => $course->modules_count ?? 0,
            'total_points' => $course->total_points ?? 0,
        ])
        ->values();

    return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses', [
        'courses' => $courses,
    ]);
}
```

(`id`, `title`, `category`, `status`, `image_url` already matched — only the four renamed ones revert to column names. This also makes `index()` consistent with `edit()`, which already sends `short_description`, `total_duration`, `modules_count`, etc.)

# Skill: laravel-best-practices

# Laravel Best Practices

Best practices for Laravel, organized as an index of rule files. Each rule file teaches what to do and why. For exact API syntax, verify with `search-docs`.

## Consistency First

Before applying any rule, check what the application already does. Laravel offers multiple valid approaches, and the best choice is the one the codebase already uses, even if another pattern would be theoretically better. Inconsistency is worse than a suboptimal pattern.

Check sibling files, related controllers, models, or tests for established patterns. If one exists, follow it. Don't introduce a second way. These rules are defaults for when no pattern exists yet, not overrides.

## How to Apply

1. Check the changed files, nearby code, project configuration, and relevant tests for established patterns. Deviate only for a correctness or security defect, and call the deviation out.
2. Map every affected concern to the rule index below. Read each mapped rule file before editing. Skip unrelated rule files.
3. Make the smallest coherent change. Keep the application's architecture and naming instead of introducing a second pattern for the same job.
4. Verify version-sensitive Laravel APIs for the installed version with `search-docs`, or inspect the installed framework when it is unavailable.
5. Run the narrowest relevant tests first, then the project's formatting and static-analysis checks when the change warrants them.
6. Re-read the diff against every mapped rule before finishing.

## Rule Index

Cross-cutting changes often need more than one rule file.

| Concern | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Query count, eager loading, indexes, large datasets | [`rules/db-performance.md`](rules/db-performance.md) |
| Subqueries, aggregates, complex ordering and query plans | [`rules/advanced-queries.md`](rules/advanced-queries.md) |
| Models, relationships, scopes, casts | [`rules/eloquent.md`](rules/eloquent.md) |
| Authentication, authorization, input safety, secrets, uploads | [`rules/security.md`](rules/security.md) |
| Form Requests and validation rules | [`rules/validation.md`](rules/validation.md) |
| Controllers, route binding, resources, middleware | [`rules/routing.md`](rules/routing.md) |
| Schema changes, columns, foreign keys, indexes | [`rules/migrations.md`](rules/migrations.md) |
| Jobs, retries, uniqueness, batches, Horizon | [`rules/queue-jobs.md`](rules/queue-jobs.md) |
| Cache lifetime, invalidation, locks, memoization | [`rules/caching.md`](rules/caching.md) |
| Outbound requests, retries, timeouts, fakes | [`rules/http-client.md`](rules/http-client.md) |
| Exceptions, reporting, rendering, log context | [`rules/error-handling.md`](rules/error-handling.md) |
| Events and notifications | [`rules/events-notifications.md`](rules/events-notifications.md) |
| Mailables and mail assertions | [`rules/mail.md`](rules/mail.md) |
| Scheduled tasks and overlap protection | [`rules/scheduling.md`](rules/scheduling.md) |
| Collections, lazy iteration, bulk operations | [`rules/collections.md`](rules/collections.md) |
| Blade components, attributes, composers | [`rules/blade-views.md`](rules/blade-views.md) |
| Environment values and application configuration | [`rules/config.md`](rules/config.md) |
| Tests: coverage, factories, fakes, and assertions | the `testing-best-practices` skill |
| Naming, helpers, file boundaries, PHP style | [`rules/style.md`](rules/style.md) |
| Actions, services, dependencies, application structure | [`rules/architecture.md`](rules/architecture.md) |

## Decision Rules

- Prefer framework features and existing application abstractions over new helpers or dependencies.
- Avoid speculative abstractions. Extract code when it creates a clear domain boundary, removes meaningful duplication, or makes behavior independently testable.
- Keep database access out of Blade views and prevent hidden N+1 queries across controllers, resources, jobs, and serialization.

1: # Routing and Controller Best Practices
2: 
3: ## Use Implicit Route Model Binding
4: 
5: Let Laravel resolve models from route parameters when the default lookup and missing-model behavior fit the endpoint.
6: 
7: Instead of manual lookup:
8: 
9: ```php
10: public function show(int $id): View
11: {
12:     $post = Post::findOrFail($id);
13: 
14:     return view('posts.show', ['post' => $post]);
15: }
16: ```
17: 
18: Use route model binding:
19: 
20: ```php
21: public function show(Post $post): View
22: {
23:     return view('posts.show', ['post' => $post]);
24: }
25: ```
26: 
27: ## Scope Nested Bindings
28: 
29: Use scoped bindings when a nested resource must belong to its parent. This constrains model resolution; it does not replace authorization.
30: 
31: ```php
32: Route::get('/users/{user}/posts/{post}', function (User $user, Post $post) {
33:     // The resolved post belongs to the resolved user.
34: })->scopeBindings();
35: ```
36: 
37: ## Use Resource Routes for Resourceful Actions
38: 
39: Use `Route::resource()` or `Route::apiResource()` when the endpoint follows Laravel's resource-controller actions. Define explicit routes when the behavior does not fit that vocabulary.
40: 
41: ```php
42: Route::resource('posts', PostController::class);
43: 
44: // Alternatively, for an API-only resource:
45: Route::apiResource('posts', ApiPostController::class);
46: ```
47: 
48: `apiResource()` omits the HTML-oriented `create` and `edit` routes. It does not itself add an `/api` prefix; that prefix comes from the application's API route configuration.
49: 
50: ## Organize Controllers Around Resources
51: 
52: As a general default, organize each controller around one resource and use Laravel's standard resource actions: `index`, `show`, `create`, `store`, `edit`, `update`, and `destroy`. This keeps routes predictable and prevents controllers from accumulating unrelated behavior.
53: 
54: When a controller needs a custom action such as `publish`, `approve`, or `archive`, first consider whether that behavior represents a separate resource. A focused resource controller gives the behavior its own authorization, validation, and middleware boundary.
55: 
56: Custom action on the primary controller:
57: 
58: ```php
59: Route::post('/podcasts/{podcast}/publish', [PodcastController::class, 'publish']);
60: ```
61: 
62: The published podcast modeled as a resource:
63: 
64: ```php
65: Route::post('/published-podcasts/{podcast}', [PublishedPodcastController::class, 'store'])
66:     ->name('published-podcasts.store');
67: 
68: Route::delete('/published-podcasts/{podcast}', [PublishedPodcastController::class, 'destroy'])
69:     ->name('published-podcasts.destroy');
70: ```
71: 
72: ```php
73: class PublishedPodcastController extends Controller
74: {
75:     public function store(Podcast $podcast): RedirectResponse
76:     {
77:         $podcast->publish();
78: 
79:         return back();
80:     }
81: 
82:     public function destroy(Podcast $podcast): RedirectResponse
83:     {
84:         $podcast->unpublish();
85: 
86:         return back();
87:     }
88: }
89: ```
90: 
91: Treat a custom verb as a design signal, not proof that another controller is required. Use query parameters for simple filtering, and keep an explicit action route when modeling the operation as a resource would obscure the domain or conflict with established project conventions.
92: 
93: ## Keep Controllers Focused on HTTP Concerns
94: 
95: Controllers should coordinate HTTP input, authorization, validation, an application operation, and the response. Extract substantial or reusable business logic, but do not introduce an action or service merely to satisfy an arbitrary line limit.
96: 
97: ```php
98: public function store(StorePostRequest $request, CreatePostAction $create): RedirectResponse
99: {
100:     $post = $create->handle($request->validated());
101: 
102:     return redirect()->route('posts.show', $post);
103: }
104: ```
105: 
106: A form request can perform validation and authorization before the controller runs. Do not repeat its rules in the controller. Keep simple, endpoint-specific validation inline when extraction would not improve reuse or clarity; see the validation rules for detailed guidance.

1: # Convention and Style Best Practices

3: ## Follow Project Naming Conventions
4: 
5: Prefer Laravel's conventions in new code, but preserve an established project convention unless a coordinated rename is worthwhile.
6: 
7: | Element | Convention | Example |
8: | --- | --- | --- |
9: | Controller | Singular resource name | `ArticleController` |
10: | Model | Singular StudlyCase | `User` |
11: | Table | Plural snake_case | `article_comments` |
12: | Pivot table | Singular model names in alphabetical order, in snake_case | `article_user` |
13: | Column | snake_case | `meta_title` |
14: | Conventional foreign key | Singular model name plus `_id`, in snake_case | `article_id` |
15: | Resource URI | Plural resource | `articles/1` |
16: | Route name | Dotted segments; snake_case within a segment when needed | `users.show_active` |
17: | Method | camelCase | `getAll` |
18: | Variable | camelCase | `$articlesWithAuthor` |
19: | Collection | Descriptive and plural | `$activeUsers` |
20: | Object | Descriptive and singular | `$activeUser` |
21: | View | kebab-case | `show-filtered.blade.php` |
22: | Configuration file | snake_case | `google_calendar.php` |
23: | Enumeration | Singular StudlyCase | `UserType` |
24: 
25: ## Prefer Clear, Idiomatic Syntax
26: 
27: Use Laravel helpers and query methods when they communicate intent more directly. Do not shorten code when the result is ambiguous or loses useful type information.
28: 
29: | More verbose | Idiomatic alternative |
30: | --- | --- |
31: | `Session::get('cart')` | `session('cart')` |
32: | `$request->session()->get('cart')` | `session('cart')` |
33: | `return Redirect::back()` | `return back()` |
34: | `Carbon::now()` | `now()` |
35: | `->where('column', '=', 1)` | `->where('column', 1)` |
36: | `->orderBy('created_at', 'desc')` | `->latest()` |
37: | `->orderBy('created_at', 'asc')` | `->oldest()` |
38: | `->first()?->name` | `->value('name')` when only that value is needed |
39: 
40: Use typed request accessors such as `$request->string()`, `$request->integer()`, and `$request->boolean()` when their coercion matches the operation.
41: 
42: ## Use Utilities When They Clarify Intent
43: 
44: Laravel's `Str`, `Arr`, `Number`, and `Uri` utilities provide expressive operations and framework-consistent behavior. Prefer them when they are clearer or safer than an equivalent PHP operation, not as an unconditional replacement for every built-in function.
45: 
46: ```php
47: $slug = Str::slug($title);
48: $short = Str::limit($text, 100);
49: $class = class_basename(User::class);
50: $result = Str::of($input)->trim()->replace('_', '-')->lower();
51: ```
52: 
53: Use `Arr` for dot notation and common transformations:
54: 
55: ```php
56: $name = Arr::get($array, 'user.name', 'default');
57: $public = Arr::only($attributes, ['name', 'email']);
58: ```
59: 
60: Use `Number` for localized display formatting rather than values that will be stored or calculated:
61: 
62: ```php
63: Number::format(1000000);
64: Number::currency(1500, 'USD');
65: Number::fileSize(1024 * 1024);
66: ```
67: 
68: Use `Uri` when constructing or transforming a uniform resource identifier (URI) benefits from a structured API:
69: 
70: ```php
71: $uri = Uri::of('https://example.com/search')
72:     ->withQuery(['q' => 'laravel', 'page' => 1]);
73: ```
74: 
75: Check the documentation for the Laravel version supported by the project before using newer utility classes or methods.
76: 
77: ## Keep Presentation Code Maintainable
78: 
79: Prefer the project's asset pipeline, components, and existing conventions for substantial JavaScript and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS). Small page-specific scripts or styles can be reasonable in Blade layouts or stacks; avoid mixing large behavior and style blocks into templates.
80: 
81: Pass server data with an encoding mechanism appropriate to its context. For example, Blade's `Js::from()` safely formats data for JavaScript:
82: 
83: ```blade
84: <script>
85:     const article = {{ Js::from($article) }};
86: </script>
87: ```
88: 
89: Data attributes are useful for small scalar values, but serializing a large model into an attribute can expose unnecessary fields and complicate escaping.
90: 
91: ## Write Comments That Explain Why
92: 
93: Prefer clear names and small units of code over comments that merely restate an operation. Add concise comments for non-obvious constraints, tradeoffs, workarounds, regular expressions, or external behavior that the code cannot express by itself. Keep comments accurate when behavior changes.
94: 
95: Unhelpful:
96: 
97: ```php
98: // Check whether the query has joins.
99: if (count((array) $builder->getQuery()->joins) > 0) {
100:     // ...
101: }
102: ```
103: 
104: Clearer:
105: 
106: ```php
107: if ($this->hasJoins()) {
108:     // ...
109: }
110: ```

# The `edit()` Method — Explained Simply

## The big picture

If `index()` is the librarian preparing **display cards**, then `edit()` is the librarian preparing a **complete working dossier** — not a summary card, but the full folder opened up on the desk: the course's own details *plus* its entire structure of modules and lessons, all arranged in the correct order, ready for the editor page to work on.

Where `index()` sends a **flat list of summaries**, `edit()` sends **one deeply detailed object** — a tree.

---

## Line 1: The signature

```php
public function edit(Course $course): Response
```

Handles `GET /dashboard/courses/{course}/edit` (route name `dashboard.courses.edit`).

Look closely at the parameter: `Course $course`. There's **no `$course = Course::find($id)` anywhere in the body**. That's route model binding doing silent work for you. Because the parameter type is `Course` and the route has `{course}`, Laravel automatically:

1. Takes the ID from the URL (say `/dashboard/courses/7/edit` → `7`)
2. Runs `Course::findOrFail(7)`
3. Hands you the resulting model — or, if course 7 doesn't exist, aborts with a 404 before your code even runs

You never wrote a database lookup line, yet one happened. It's like a receptionist who checks you in before your meeting — you just show up and the guest is already seated.

---

## Lines 2–4: Loading the tree

```php
$course->load([
    'modules' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id'),
    'modules.lessons' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index')->orderBy('id'),
]);
```

This is **eager loading** — the most important concept in this method. Let me explain it slowly.

The `$course` model knows *how* to fetch its modules (`$course->modules`) — that's the `hasMany` relationship defined in the model. But that relationship is **lazy**: it doesn't touch the database until the moment you ask for it. And if you asked for modules *one course at a time, one module's lessons at a time*, you'd get the classic **N+1 problem**:

- 1 query for the course
- 1 query for its modules
- then **1 query per module** for that module's lessons

5 modules? 7 queries. 50 modules? 52 queries. Each round-trip to the database is real time spent.

`load()` fixes this. Reading the array argument in plain English:

- **`'modules' => ...`** — "fetch ALL modules for this course, and while you're at it, sort them by `order_index` (their drag-and-drop position), breaking ties by `id` (creation order)"
- **`'modules.lessons' => ...`** — "also, for every module you just fetched, fetch ALL its lessons — same sorting rule"

The dot notation (`modules.lessons`) means "one level deeper." Eloquent translates this into a **small fixed number of queries** (here: one for modules, one for all lessons), no matter how many modules exist. 5 modules or 500 — the query count stays the same.

The arrow functions (`fn ($query) => ...`) are **query customizers**. Eager loading by itself would fetch rows in arbitrary database order — dangerous, because the editor's module list could render scrambled. Each closure receives the pending query and bolts on an `ORDER BY` before it executes. The double sort (`order_index` then `id`) is the tiebreaker story from the reorder explanation: position first, and if two things share a position, older-created first.

After this line, `$course` is like a folder with everything clipped inside it — no more trips to the filing cabinet needed.

---

## Lines 5–6: Starting the payload

```php
return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Courses/Editor', [
    'course' => [
```

Same as `index()`: render the React page at `resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Courses/Editor/index.jsx` and hand it props. But this time the prop is one big structured `course` object. Everything from here down is just *building that object by hand* — the same whitelisting idea as `index()`: the page gets exactly these fields and nothing else.

---

## The scalar fields (course's own columns)

```php
'id' => $course->id,
'title' => $course->title ?? '',
'category' => $course->category ?? '',
'short_description' => $course->short_description ?? '',
'long_description' => $course->long_description ?? '',
'status' => $course->status,
```

- **`id`** — needed for the save/delete endpoints and the draft store key (`useCourseDraftStore` caches drafts per course id).
- **`title` / `category` / descriptions** — note every nullable field gets `?? ''`. Why normalize to empty string here, when `index()` used a *display fallback* (`'Untitled Course'`)? Because this data is going into **form inputs**. An `<input>` needs a string — `null` would make React complain about uncontrolled-to-controlled switching. `''` is the correct "empty input" value. This is the difference between *data for display* (fallback text is fine) and *data for editing* (raw-but-normalized is right).
- **`status`** — `'draft'` or `'published'`, drives the editor's status toggle.

---

## The image (our new inline version)

```php
'image_url' => $course->image_url
    ? Storage::disk('public')->url($course->image_url)
    : null,
```

Read it as: *"if a cover image path exists, turn it into a full browser-usable URL; otherwise null."* The editor uses this only for the **preview** of the current image — the actual replacement happens through a file upload on save, handled by `syncCoverImage()` in `update()`.

---

## The stats block

```php
'total_duration' => $course->total_duration,
'modules_count' => $course->modules_count,
'lessons_count' => $course->lessons_count,
'total_points' => $course->total_points,
```

Same denormalized "numbers written on the folder cover" from `index()` — read directly, never recomputed. The editor displays them in the left panel as read-only stats (`courseStats` object). Note: no `?? 0` fallbacks here unlike `index()` — a slight inconsistency, harmless since the columns are `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`.

Fun observation: `modules_count` is actually **redundant data** here — the full `modules` array is being sent right below it, so the frontend *could* just count it. But it's sent anyway because it's already denormalized on the row — free to read, no extra query.

---

## The nested tree — modules containing lessons

```php
'modules' => $course->modules->map(fn (Module $module): array => [
    'id' => $module->id,
    'title' => $module->title,
    'lessons' => $module->lessons->map(fn (Lesson $lesson): array => [
        'id' => $lesson->id,
        'title' => $lesson->title,
        'type' => $lesson->type,
    ])->values()->all(),
])->values()->all(),
```

This is `map` inside `map` — a **two-level transformation**. Breaking it down:

**Outer map (per module):** each Eloquent `Module` model → a plain array with three keys: `id`, `title`, and `lessons`. Notice a module sends *far less* than a course: no order, no timestamps, no stats. The outline only needs identity, label, and children — this is the whitelist principle applied at every level of the tree.

**Inner map (per lesson):** each `Lesson` → array with `id`, `title`, `type`. The `type` (`article`/`quiz`/`exam`) matters because the outline renders a different icon per lesson type.

**`->values()->all()`** — you know `values()` already (guarantee JSON array). The `.all()` after it is new: it converts the Laravel Collection into a **plain PHP array**. Collections serialize fine too, but `.all()` says "this is finished, plain data now" — nested all the way down.

The important invisible detail: `$module->lessons` here triggers **no extra query**. The eager load earlier already fetched all lessons in one batch and clipped them onto their modules. Accessing the relationship now just reads from memory. *That's* why the `load()` at the top exists — this bottom section would be an N+1 disaster without it.

The resulting JSON the React editor receives:

```js
course = {
    id, title, category, ..., total_points,
    modules: [
        { id: 10, title: 'Introduction', lessons: [
            { id: 1001, title: 'Skim Reading', type: 'article' },
            { id: 1003, title: 'Speed Test',   type: 'quiz' },
        ]},
        { id: 20, title: 'Paragraph Structure', lessons: [...] },
    ]
}
```

This is exactly the shape `CourseContent.jsx` renders as the drag-and-drop outline.

---

## What `edit()` deliberately does NOT do

Understanding by omission:

1. **No saving** — it only *reads*. Saving is `update()`'s job (PUT). `edit()` = show the form, `update()` = receive the form.
2. **No recalculation** — stats are read off the row. If drift ever existed, the editor would display wrong numbers with total confidence.
3. **No lesson content** — notice lessons send only `title` and `type`, **not** `article_content` or questions. Full lesson content lives in the *separate* standalone lesson editor (`LessonController::edit`). The course editor is an **outline view** — you see the tree structure, and click into a lesson to edit its body. One page, one job.

---

## One breath summary

> *"Take the course from the URL; clip on all its modules and their lessons in one batch, already sorted; hand the editor a hand-built tree: course details as form-ready strings, stats off the row's cover, and a lean module/lesson outline — nothing more."*

And the one design note for your ongoing redesign: this method, like `index()`, is a **pure consumer of denormalized stats** — but unlike `index()`, it also sends the *actual tree* the stats summarize. That makes it a nice cross-check candidate: `modules_count` vs `modules.length` should always agree. If you ever move to computed-at-read-time stats, this method could derive the counts from the already-loaded tree for free — one less thing that can drift.

The user asks: why after ordering by `order_index`, is it ordered again by `id`?

This is the tiebreaker question. Let me explain simply:

1. `order_index` is the drag-and-drop position (0, 1, 2, ...). It's supposed to be unique *in practice* but nothing in the database enforces uniqueness — there's no unique constraint on (module_id, order_index) or (course_id, order_index).

2. Situations where two rows can share the same `order_index`:
   - Default value: new rows are created with `order_index` default 0. The store() methods do set max+1, but...
   - Subset reorder requests (as I explained earlier): if a hand-crafted PATCH sends only some IDs, the others keep old indexes → duplicates possible
   - Race conditions: two concurrent creates computing the same max+1
   - Historical drift: manual DB edits, seeder mistakes
   - The reorder update doesn't enforce completeness

3. Without a tiebreaker, when two rows have the same order_index, the database returns them in **arbitrary order** — SQLite specifically makes NO guarantee about row order for equal keys; it depends on the query plan, how rows physically sit in pages, index usage, etc. So the same query could return different orderings on different days or with different SQLite versions/plans.

4. Arbitrary order in a UI = the outline items could **jump around/shuffle randomly** between page loads. Deterministic UI requires a total ordering.

5. `id` is autoincrement — strictly increasing over time, so it's a proxy for creation order: among items with the same position, the older-created one appears first. It's stable, unique, always present. So `ORDER BY order_index, id` produces a **total order** — every pair of rows has a defined sequence, guaranteed repeatable on every load.

6. Why does this matter operationally in this app? When duplicates exist, the read side is stable (won't shuffle), and after any drag (full-list reorder) the positions get rewritten densely 0..n-1 anyway, which self-heals duplicates. Also delete reindexes densely. So the id tiebreaker is a cheap safety net: stable display + graceful handling of inconsistent data.

7. Could they use something else? Alternatives: created_at (not unique either, second precision — two rows created in the same second still tie; id is better), a unique composite index (course_id, order_index) — enforces uniqueness but makes reorder writes more complex (swap ordering issues, deferred constraints), fractional ordering (LexoRank style), etc. id-as-tiebreaker is the simplest robust choice and a common Laravel idiom.

Let me also tie to the earlier reorder discussion: I mentioned in the reorder explanation "Read-side tiebreaker is orderBy('id')" and the subset-request scenario. This question follows up on that.

- what ORDER BY does with ties (undefined)
- how ties can happen here (list the realistic paths)

- result: total deterministic order + self-healing behavior

Great question — this is the **tiebreaker**, and it exists because of a hard truth about databases: **when two rows tie on the sort key, the database promises you nothing about their order.**

## The problem: `order_index` can have duplicates

The schema does not enforce uniqueness on `order_index`. Nothing stops two modules in the same course from both having `order_index = 2`. And duplicates are not hypothetical — there are realistic ways they happen:

**1. Subset reorder requests.** Remember the reorder endpoint accepts *any* list of valid IDs — it doesn't verify the list covers every module. A hand-crafted PATCH sending only `[moduleC, moduleA]` renumbers those two to `0, 1`, while the untouched modules keep their old indexes. Now `moduleB` still has `1` — same as `moduleA`. Duplicate.

**2. Creation races.** `store()` computes the next position as `max(order_index) + 1` in PHP. If two requests create a module at nearly the same moment, both may read the same `max`, both write the same `order_index`. (SQLite's write lock makes this unlikely, but the code doesn't guard it.)

**3. Any manual data edit or seeder mistake.** The columns are plain integers with a default of `0` — insert a few rows bypassing the controller and you can easily create several `0`s.

## What happens WITHOUT a tiebreaker

Suppose two modules both have `order_index = 1`. Your query says:

```sql
ORDER BY order_index
```

SQLite (and SQL in general) says: *"for equal keys, I'll give them to you in whatever order I happen to produce them."* That depends on internal storage layout, the query plan, whether a scan or an index is used — **it can differ between runs**. It's not random noise you'd necessarily catch in testing; it can be stable for weeks on your machine and then flip after a migration, a VACUUM, or a data change.

In the UI, this means the outline could silently **reshuffle between page loads** — module 2 and module 3 swapping places for no visible reason. For a drag-and-drop editor, that's poison: the user drags things to positions, so the display must be *deterministic* — same data, same order, every single time.

## What `id` adds

```sql
ORDER BY order_index ASC, id ASC
```

Sorting works left-to-right: `order_index` decides first; **only when it ties does `id` step in**. And `id` is the perfect referee because it is:

- **Unique** — an autoincrement primary key can never tie, so the combined sort is a *total order*: every possible pair of rows has exactly one settled sequence
- **Always present** — never null, never missing
- **Meaningful** — autoincrement means bigger id = created later, so among items with the same position, *the older one shows first*. That's the most intuitive resolution ("things that were there first stay on top")

Result: same data → same order → same screen. Guaranteed.

## The nice side effect: self-healing

The tiebreaker also makes duplicates **harmless and temporary**. The moment the admin drags anything, the frontend sends the full ordered ID list, the backend rewrites positions densely as `0, 1, 2, … N-1` — and the duplicates are simply gone. Same after a delete, which reindexes survivors. So the app's contract is:

> *"Positions might occasionally collide; while they do, display stays stable (id breaks the tie); the next drag or delete repairs them."*

That's a much simpler world than enforcing uniqueness — a unique constraint on `(course_id, order_index)` would make reorder writes genuinely awkward (you can't naively renumber in place without transient duplicates, so you'd need careful update ordering or deferred constraints).

## Why not `created_at` instead of `id`?

It's the obvious alternative ("older first"), but timestamps aren't unique — two modules created within the same second still tie, and *both* are nullable in principle. `id` gives you the same "creation order" meaning with hard uniqueness. That's why `orderBy('id')` as the second sort key is a standard Laravel idiom — you'll see it in both eager loads here, and in the sibling reindex loops in the destroy methods, for exactly the same reason.

You're right about the relationship — one course has many modules, each module belongs to exactly one course. And yes, the query only fetches **this course's** modules. But that's not what the tiebreaker is for. Let me explain with a simple picture.

## The lineup analogy

Imagine this course's modules are students lining up for a class photo. Each student holds a number card that says their spot in the line: 0, 1, 2, 3…

Sorting by `order_index` means: *"line up by the number on your card."* Works perfectly… **as long as no two students hold the same number.**

But nothing stops two students from both holding a card that says **1**. Maybe the teacher made a mistake handing out cards (a reorder that only renumbered some rows), or two students grabbed cards at the same moment (two modules created at once).

When two cards match, the photographer — the database — has **no rule** for who stands in front. It's not being difficult on purpose; the instruction "sort by card number" simply says nothing about this case. So it puts them in whatever order it feels like, which can even change from day to day. In the app, that would look like **two modules silently swapping places between page loads**.

The second sort key fixes it with one extra sentence: *"if your cards match, the one who joined the class earlier (smaller `id`) stands first."*

Now every situation has an answer. Same data → same line → same screen, every time.

## Why "but we only fetch this course's modules" doesn't prevent this

Because the tie happens **inside** that small group. Look — here's one course's three modules, all correctly belonging to it:

| module | order_index | id |
|---|---|---|
| A — "Introduction" | 0 | 12 |
| B — "Paragraphs" | 1 | 13 |
| C — "Vocabulary" | 1 | **14** ← same card as B |

Scoping already did its job — no other course's modules are in this list. The problem is purely B vs C: both belong here, and both claim spot 1. Even a set of three rows can contain a tie. The `id` tiebreaker only ever gets consulted **between rows that are already in the same list and already tied** — it never compares across courses.

## In one sentence

- The relationship (`WHERE course_id = ...`) decides **who is in the line**.
- `order_index` decides **where in the line** they stand.
- `id` is the backup rule for the rare case two of them claim the same spot — so the line never looks different on two different days.

What you're describing is a **composite unique constraint** — "per course, each position number can be used by at most one module." In schema terms: `unique(course_id, order_index)`. It's a great instinct: it moves the "no two cards with the same number" rule from *convention* (code promises it) to *guarantee* (database refuses to break it). But it has one sharp edge that touches the reorder code — let me explain, then give you the plan.

## The catch: reordering collides with itself mid-update

Here's the problem in miniature. Current state:

| module | order_index |
|---|---|
| A | 0 |
| B | 1 |
| C | 2 |

The user drags **C to the front**. The endpoint loops through `[C, A, B]` and assigns `0, 1, 2`:

```php
foreach ($validated['module_ids'] as $index => $moduleId) {
    // update ... set order_index = $index
}
```

- Update C → `0`. But **A already sits at 0**. 💥 Unique constraint rejects the write.

Note the absurdity: the *final* state is perfectly legal — it's only the *middle* of the process that's illegal. The database checks after every single update, not after the whole loop. (The transaction doesn't save you here — SQLite checks uniqueness immediately per statement.)

## The fix: park everyone out of the way first

The classic two-phase move, still inside one transaction:

```php
// Phase 1 — shift ALL positions up by N (out of the target range):
//   A→3, B→4, C→5   (still unique, since the old values were unique)
Module::query()
    ->where('course_id', $course->id)
    ->update(['order_index' => DB::raw('order_index + '.$count)]);

// Phase 2 — assign final seats 0,1,2… (range the old values can't reach)
foreach ($validated['module_ids'] as $index => $moduleId) { ... }
```

Parking high instead of low because the column is `unsignedInteger` (no negatives). Two extra lines, collision becomes impossible by construction.

## Audit of every other writer of `order_index`

I traced all the paths so you don't get surprise explosions later:

| Write path | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `store()` (append new module/lesson) | ✅ Safe — `max + 1` is by definition an unused number |
| `destroy()` (reindex survivors `0,1,2…`) | ✅ Safe — after a delete every survivor only moves *down*, and the loop walks front-to-back, so each seat being filled was just vacated. (Only holds once duplicates can't exist — which the constraint itself guarantees.) |
| `reorder()` endpoints | ⚠️ Needs the two-phase fix above |
| `syncQuestions()` (lesson save) | ✅ Safe — old rows are deleted first, fresh inserts get `0,1,2…` |
| Seeders | ✅ Look clean (positions restart per parent in every seeder) — will verify during implementation |
| **Factories** | ⚠️ Real gotcha — tests create multiple modules/lessons per parent; if factories randomize `order_index`, they'll start throwing unique violations. They must be made sequential per parent. |

## The plan

1. **Add unique constraints** — the open question is how far down the tree (below).
2. **Two-phase reorder** in `ModuleController::reorder` and `LessonController::reorder`
3. **Tighten reorder validation** — with uniqueness, a *partial* id list becomes ill-defined (which numbers do the missing rows get?). The endpoints should now require the **complete** list: reject with 422 if `count(ids)` ≠ parent's child count. The frontend already always sends the full list, so this costs nothing and matches the constraint.
4. **Fix factories** to generate sequential positions per parent
5. **Keep the `orderBy('id')` tiebreaker** — with uniqueness guaranteed it's technically redundant, but it's free, harmless, and stays as a safety net (recommend keeping)
6. **Tests** — extend `CoursesManagementTest`: drag-last-to-front (the exact collision case), partial-list rejection, and duplicate-position rejection. I'll read the testing skill before writing them.
7. Pint + full courses test file

Good instinct — but splice solves the wrong half of the problem. Let me show you why.

## Splice is already doing its job — on the frontend

`arrayMove` from dnd-kit **is** a splice: it cuts the dragged item out of the array and reinserts it at the new index. By the time the backend receives `module_ids: [C, A, B]`, the *computation* is finished. The backend doesn't need to figure out the new order — it's been handed the final answer as a plain list.

The hard part is **writing that answer into the database** when the database has a rule that says "no two rows of the same course may share a position number." And no PHP array operation can help there, because the collision isn't in your array — it's *between the UPDATE statements* as the database executes them one by one.

## The musical chairs problem

Take the smallest interesting case. Current seats:

| seat | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| sitting | A | B | C |

The user dragged C to the front. Target:

| seat | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| sitting | C | A | B |

Now try to perform this with single moves, in **any** order you like:

- Move C to seat 0? **A is sitting there.** 💥
- Move A to seat 1? **B is sitting there.** 💥
- Move B to seat 2? **C is sitting there.** 💥

Every person's destination is occupied by *another person who also needs to move*. It's a circle: C wants A's seat, A wants B's, B wants C's. There is no free chair to start the dance. You can splice, sort, reverse, or shuffle your PHP arrays all day — the moment you write these three moves to the database one at a time, the first move always hits an occupied chair.

You've met this problem before in its smallest form:

```php
$temp = $a;      // you can't swap two variables without a third
$a = $b;
$b = $temp;
```

Swapping two values needs a scratch variable. Reassigning N seats needs a scratch *seat*. That's all the "park high" phase is — the generalized temp variable:

```
Phase 1: everyone stands on the sidelines   (A→3, B→4, C→5)
Phase 2: everyone sits in their new chair   (C→0, A→1, B→2)
```

One extra `UPDATE` for the whole batch, and the collision becomes impossible by construction.

## What about the clever alternatives?

They all exist, and they all still need the same scratch:

- **Pairwise swaps** ("swap A↔C, then A↔B") — each swap itself needs a temp seat, so you're parking per-swap instead of once per batch. More code, same idea.
- **Cycle rotation with one spare seat** — the classic in-place algorithm: detect the cycles in the permutation, park just *one* member per cycle, rotate the rest. Works, but you'd be writing cycle-decomposition code in PHP to save a single `UPDATE` on a table with a handful of rows. Cleverness with no payoff.
- **`upsert()`** — still processes rows one at a time under the same unique index; same collision, just hidden inside a fancier statement.
- **Delete and re-insert** (like the lesson save does) — dodges the constraint, but at the cost of regenerating every module/lesson ID. That's the exact disease we've been trying to cure in this codebase.

## So the plan stands

The two-phase reorder isn't a workaround for a bad design — it *is* the standard way to permute a uniquely-constrained column. Splice already did its part on the React side; the park-then-place pair does the database's part. Everything else in the plan (constraints on all 4 levels, full-list validation, factory audit, tests) is unchanged.

## 2. `ModuleController::reorder` — full-list validation + two-phase write

```php
public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course): RedirectResponse
{
    $validated = $request->validate([
        'module_ids' => [
            'required',
            'array',
            'min:1',
            function (string $attribute, mixed $value, Closure $fail) use ($course) {
                if (count($value) !== $course->modules()->count()) {
                    $fail('The module ids must list every module in the course.');
                }
            },
        ],
        'module_ids.*' => [
            'required',
            'integer',
            'distinct',
            Rule::exists('modules', 'id')->where('course_id', $course->id),
        ],
    ]);

    DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $validated): void {
        $count = count($validated['module_ids']);

        // Park every position above the target range first — with the
        // unique (course_id, order_index) index, assigning final seats
        // 0..N-1 directly could collide with rows not yet moved.
        Module::query()
            ->where('course_id', $course->id)
            ->update(['order_index' => DB::raw('order_index + '.$count)]);

        foreach ($validated['module_ids'] as $index => $moduleId) {
            Module::query()
                ->where('course_id', $course->id)
                ->whereKey($moduleId)
                ->update(['order_index' => $index]);
        }
    });

    return back();
}
```

Add `use Closure;` to the imports.

**Why parking is required:** dense unique positions mean any real change contains a cycle (C wants A's seat, A wants B's, B wants C's) — no ordering of plain updates avoids an occupied seat. Parking high is the generalized temp variable. High range because the column is `unsignedInteger`.

**Why the full-list rule:** with uniqueness, a partial id list is ill-defined (what numbers do the unlisted rows get?). The frontend already always sends the full list (`reordered.map(m => m.id)`), so this changes nothing for the UI — it just makes the API honest.

# Skill: testing-best-practices

# Testing Best Practices

This skill provides rules for designing Laravel tests. Each rule file explains what to do and why. Use `search-docs` for Laravel and Pest API syntax.
This project uses Pest. Follow the corresponding guidance in each rule.

## Consistency First

Read nearby tests before you choose syntax and organization.

A pattern repeated throughout the project is a convention, and project conventions take precedence over this skill. Follow them and give new tests the same structure.

These rules govern the tests you write now. An existing test that follows a project convention is not defective merely because it conflicts with this skill. Do not delete or rewrite it. If the convention has drawbacks, explain them and let the user decide.

## What to Test

Read this section before you write a test.

- Test observable behavior and application contracts. A test must pass after an implementation change if the behavior stays the same.
- Cover every changed decision and each applicable high-value failure mode. A decision is a branch, a validation, a calculation, or an authorization.
- Exercise declarations through behavior instead of repeating their text.
- Leave framework behavior to framework tests. Testing project configuration is not testing the framework. A constrained relationship, cast, scope, or validation rule belongs to this project.
- Keep every test that can detect a distinct defect. When two tests detect the same defect, trim the higher-layer test to one case and report the duplication. Do not delete an existing test.
- Write a feature test first. Write a unit test only for logic that does not use the framework.
- Write a feature test for every behavior reachable through a request. Real-browser tests require `pestphp/pest-plugin-browser` and a browser download, neither of which this project installs. Mention the package only if the user asks for a real-browser test.
- Judge an architecture test by the convention it protects, not by the rules above. An `arch()` test declares a rule for an entire directory, such as the parent class of every model, the classes that may use an enum, or the methods every factory declares. It intentionally checks declarations and fails when a new file breaks the convention.
- Use the test tools that the project installs. Add a new test dependency, plugin, or browser only after the user asks for it.

## How to Apply

1. Read the code under test. Read the tests in the same directory. Identify every decision in the code.
2. Select every applicable branch in the rule index. Read every selected rule file.
3. Report each defect in the code before you write a test. Examples are a method with no body, a policy that no action calls, and a write action with no validation. Test the actual behavior. Report the defect to the user.
4. Write the tests. Run the smallest set of tests that covers the change. The tests must pass.
5. Check every applicable item in `rules/review.md` and every selected rule file. Resolve every mismatch before completion.

## Rule Index

Most changes need more than one rule file.

| Subject | Rule File |
| --- | --- |
| Test framework features that may already do the work | [`rules/finding-features.md`](rules/finding-features.md) |
| File layout, test names, and groups | [`rules/naming.md`](rules/naming.md) |
| Arrange-act-assert and choosing the correct assertion | [`rules/assertions.md`](rules/assertions.md) |
| Endpoint coverage, authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, validation, and browser tests | [`rules/endpoint-tests.md`](rules/endpoint-tests.md) |
| Factories, test data ownership, and repeated input values | [`rules/test-data.md`](rules/test-data.md) |
| Fakes, mocks, outbound HTTP, time, randomness, and databases | [`rules/isolation.md`](rules/isolation.md) |
| Escaping, injection, cross-tenant access, and privilege checks | [`rules/security.md`](rules/security.md) |
| Environment and CI settings for a slow suite | [`rules/performance.md`](rules/performance.md) |
| Reviewing a test or suite | [`rules/review.md`](rules/review.md) |

New method:
```php
    /**
     * Persist a new display order for the course's modules.
     */
    public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course): RedirectResponse
    {
        $validated = $request->validate([
            'module_ids' => [
                'required',
                'array',
                'min:1',
                function (string $attribute, mixed $value, Closure $fail) use ($course) {
                    if (count($value) !== $course->modules()->count()) {
                        $fail('The module ids must list every module in the course.');
                    }
                },
            ],
            'module_ids.*' => [
                'required',
                'integer',
                'distinct',
                Rule::exists('modules', 'id')->where('course_id', $course->id),
            ],
        ]);

        DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $validated): void {
            $count = count($validated['module_ids']);

            // Park every position above the target range first —
            // with unique (course_id, order_index), assigning the
            // final 0..N-1 seats directly could collide with rows
            // that have not moved yet.
            Module::query()
                ->where('course_id', $course->id)
                ->update(['order_index' => DB::raw('order_index + '.$count)]);

            foreach ($validated['module_ids'] as $index => $moduleId) {
                Module::query()
                    ->where('course_id', $course->id)
                    ->whereKey($moduleId)
                    ->update(['order_index' => $index]);
            }
        });

        return back();
    }
```

```php
test('module reorder moves the last module to the front under unique positions', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    $moduleA = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    $moduleB = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 1]);
    $moduleC = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 2]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.reorder', $course), [
            'module_ids' => [$moduleC->id, $moduleA->id, $moduleB->id],
        ])
        ->assertRedirect();

    expect($moduleC->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(0)
        ->and($moduleA->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1)
        ->and($moduleB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(2);
});

test('module reorder rejects a partial id list', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    $moduleB = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 1]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.reorder', $course), [
            'module_ids' => [$moduleB->id],
        ])
        ->assertInvalid('module_ids');

    expect($moduleB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1);
});

test('lesson reorder rejects a partial id list', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    $module = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    Lesson::factory()->article()->create(['course_id' => $course->id, 'module_id' => $module->id, 'order_index' => 0]);
    $lessonB = Lesson::factory()->article()->create(['course_id' => $course->id, 'module_id' => $module->id, 'order_index' => 1]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.reorder', [$course, $module]), [
            'lesson_ids' => [$lessonB->id],
        ])
        ->assertInvalid('lesson_ids');

    expect($lessonB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1);
});

test('database rejects duplicate order positions within the same parent', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);

    expect(fn () => Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]))
        ->toThrow(QueryException::class);
});
```

  "newString": "    /**\n     * Persist a new display order for the module's lessons.\n     */\n    public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course, Module $module): RedirectResponse\n    {\n        $validated = $request->validate([\n            'lesson_ids' => [\n                'required',\n                'array',\n                'min:1',\n                function (string $attribute, mixed $value, Closure $fail) use ($module) {\n                    if (count($value) !== $module->lessons()->count()) {\n                        $fail('The lesson ids must list every lesson in the module.');\n                    }\n                },\n            ],\n            'lesson_ids.*' => [\n                'required',\n                'integer',\n                'distinct',\n                Rule::exists('lessons', 'id')->where('module_id', $module->id),\n            ],\n        ]);\n\n        DB::transaction(function () use ($module, $validated): void {\n            $count = count($validated['lesson_ids']);\n\n            // Park every position above the target range first — with\n            // the unique (module_id, order_index) index, assigning the\n            // final 0..N-1 seats directly would collide with rows\n            // that have not moved yet.\n            Lesson::query()\n                ->where('module_id', $module->id)\n                ->update(['order_index' => DB::raw('order_index + '.$count)]);\n\n            foreach ($validated['lesson_ids'] as $index => $lessonId) {\n                Lesson::query()\n                    ->where('module_id', $module->id)\n                    ->whereKey($lessonId)\n                    ->update(['order_index' => $index]);\n            }\n        });\n\n        return back();\n    }",

```php
test('module reorder moves the last module to the front under unique positions', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    $moduleA = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    $moduleB = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 1]);
    $moduleC = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 2]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.reorder', $course), [
            'module_ids' => [$moduleC->id, $moduleA->id, $moduleB->id],
        ])
        ->assertRedirect();

    expect($moduleC->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(0)
        ->and($moduleA->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1)
        ->and($moduleB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(2);
});

test('module reorder rejects a partial id list', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    $moduleB = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 1]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.reorder', $course), [
            'module_ids' => [$moduleB->id],
        ])
        ->assertInvalid('module_ids');

    expect($moduleB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1);
});

test('lesson reorder rejects a partial id list', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    $module = Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);
    Lesson::factory()->article()->create(['course_id' => $course->id, 'module_id' => $module->id, 'order_index' => 0]);
    $lessonB = Lesson::factory()->article()->create(['course_id' => $course->id, 'module_id' => $module->id, 'order_index' => 1]);

    $this->actingAs($this->admin)
        ->patch(route('dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.reorder', [$course, $module]), [
            'lesson_ids' => [$lessonB->id],
        ])
        ->assertInvalid('lesson_ids');

    expect($lessonB->fresh()->order_index)->toBe(1);
});

test('database rejects duplicate order positions within the same parent', function () {
    $course = Course::factory()->draft()->create();
    Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]);

    expect(fn () => Module::factory()->for($course)->create(['order_index' => 0]))
        ->toThrow(QueryException::class);
});
```
