Good question — let's examine what **`spatie/eloquent-sortable`** (the package you mean) actually does, because it maps *partially* onto our problem, and there's one hard collision with the system we just built.

## What the package does

You add a `SortableTrait` to a model, and it gives you:

| Feature | What we hand-rolled |
|---|---|
| **Auto-assign order on create** — new rows get `highest + 1` automatically | our `max('order_index') ?? -1) + 1` in `store()` |
| **An ordering scope** — `$model::sorted()` for queries | our `->orderBy('order_index')` in the eager loads |
| **`setSortableOrder($ids)`** — takes an ordered id list and writes positions | our reorder endpoint's write phase |
| **Per-parent support** — override `buildSortQuery()` | our `where('course_id', ...)` scoping |

So on paper it covers everything. But look closely at `setSortableOrder` — its actual implementation is:

```php
foreach ($ids as $id) {
    $model = static::find($id);
    $model->update([$orderColumnName => $startOrder++]);   // one row at a time
}
```

**Sequential, one-row-at-a-time updates. Exactly the naive loop we replaced.**

## The collision with what we just built

Run it on our example. Intro=0, Grammar=1, Quiz=2, drag Quiz to front, list `[Quiz, Intro, Grammar]`:

| Spatie writes | Database state | Rule check |
|---|---|---|
| Quiz → 0 | **Intro 0**, Grammar 1, Quiz **0** | 💥 two modules at seat 0 |

The unique constraint we deliberately added two rounds ago — the one that made the database *guarantee* "no two modules share a seat" — **rejects Spatie's writes**. The package was designed for the simple world: a plain order column, **no unique index**. Our world is stricter than the package assumes.

Also, minor but real: Spatie numbers from **1** by default (we're 0-based), and `setSortableOrder` **silently skips** ids it can't find — our FormRequest validation (complete list, distinct, parent-scoped) is still needed, package or no package.

## The three ways to answer "can we use it?"

**Option A — Adopt it, drop the unique constraints.** Cleanest integration. But we'd be *removing the database-level guarantee you explicitly asked for* ("I am meaning to make order_index unique per course") to accommodate a package whose write pattern is weaker than our current one. Reordering would also no longer be atomic — Spatie updates rows one at a time outside any transaction, so a mid-loop crash leaves the sequence half-moved.

**Option B — Adopt it, keep the constraints, override `setSortableOrder`.** We keep the parking maneuver — but now inside an override of the package's method. The trait still gives us auto-order-on-create and the `sorted()` scope. But we're maintaining a dependency to use ~20% of it, and rewriting its core to be *stricter* than it is.

**Option C — Keep the hand-rolled version (my recommendation).** Everything Spatie offers, our code already does — plus the unique-constraint safety, transactional atomicity, and the validated full-list contract. Our total reorder machinery is ~30 lines. The package's real audience is greenfield apps with global (not per-parent) ordering and no uniqueness enforcement. Also two practical gates: the project rules require explicit approval before changing dependencies, and we'd need to verify the package's current version even supports **Laravel 13** (`composer require` would tell us immediately — support for the brand-new framework version is not guaranteed).

## My honest take

The hand-rolled version isn't less elegant than Spatie — it's the *stricter* version of the same idea. Spatie would simplify `store()`'s one-line max computation and the two `orderBy` calls, at the cost of a new dependency, an overridden core method, and (in Option A) giving up the uniqueness guarantee and atomicity you deliberately added. The elegance you're looking for isn't in a package — it's already in the parking dance, which is the industry-standard answer to this exact problem.

```php
    /**
     * Persist a new display order for the module's lessons.
     */
    public function reorder(Request $request, Course $course, Module $module): RedirectResponse
    {
        $validated = $request->validate([
            'lesson_ids' => [
                'required',
                'array',
                'min:1',
                function (string $attribute, mixed $value, Closure $fail) use ($module) {
                    if (count($value) !== $module->lessons()->count()) {
                        $fail('The lesson ids must list every lesson in the module.');
                    }
                },
            ],
            'lesson_ids.*' => [
                'required',
                'integer',
                'distinct',
                Rule::exists('lessons', 'id')->where('module_id', $module->id),
            ],
        ]);

        DB::transaction(function () use ($module, $validated): void {
            $count = count($validated['lesson_ids']);

            // Park every position above the target range first — with
            // the unique (module_id, order_index) index, assigning the
            // final 0..N-1 seats directly would collide with rows
            // that have not moved yet.
            Lesson::query()
                ->where('module_id', $module->id)
                ->update(['order_index' => DB::raw('order_index + '.$count)]);

            foreach ($validated['lesson_ids'] as $index => $lessonId) {
                Lesson::query()
                    ->where('module_id', $module->id)
                    ->whereKey($lessonId)
                    ->update(['order_index' => $index]);
            }
        });

        return back();
    }
```

**1. `ModuleObserver` gains a `deleted` hook:**

```php
/**

 * are removed — a cheap -1 instead of a full recompute.
 */
```

```php
{
    $module->course->decrement('modules_count');
}
```

Exact mirror of the `created` hook: one atomic `SET modules_count = modules_count - 1`, on the hydrated course model (not the query-builder form) so `updated_at` gets touched — preserving the "recently edited course floats to the top of the list" behavior that `recalculateStats()` used to provide.

**2. `ModuleController::destroy` drops the recalc call:**

```php

    $module->delete();

    $remaining = $course->modules()
        ->orderBy('order_index')
        ->get(['id', 'order_index']);
```

## Why the details work

- **Timing is safe** — the `deleted` event fires the instant `$module->delete()` runs, *inside* the transaction. Delete + decrement + reindex all commit or roll back together.
- **`$module->course` still resolves after deletion** — the row is gone, but the in-memory model still holds `course_id`, so the lazy-load fetches the course fine.
- **Course-level cascade is unaffected** — deleting a whole course kills modules via the *database's* `ON DELETE CASCADE`, which never fires Eloquent events. No phantom decrements for a course that's dying anyway. (Same reason seeding with `insert()` never triggered the `created` hook.)
- **The reindex loop keeps its proven safety** — survivors hold distinct seats (the unique constraint guarantees it), and renumbering only ever moves rows *down*, processed front-to-back. No parking needed here.
- **Tests pass as-is** — the module CRUD test traces: course starts at 0 → two stores → observer makes it 2 → one destroy → observer makes 1 → asserts `modules_count === 1` ✓.

## One honest footnote

`decrement()` doesn't floor at zero — if `modules_count` ever drifted below reality, a destroy could theoretically drive it to -1. With the observer pair now maintaining the count from both directions (and the constraint work having repaired the data), drift shouldn't occur; but it's the one assumption this cheap delta makes that the full recompute didn't.

## Scope note

After this, `Course::recalculateStats()` survives only in the **LessonController** paths (`store`/`update`/`destroy`), where lessons touch three counters (`lessons_count`, `total_duration`, `total_points`). The eventual `LessonObserver` equivalent is straightforward — `decrement('lessons_count')` plus `decrement('total_duration', $lesson->duration)` and `decrement('total_points', $lesson->points)` — but that's the next phase, not this one.

## Your question, answered

For a **blank new lesson**, you're essentially right — `lessons_count` is the only counter that meaningfully moves:

- `total_points`: a blank lesson has `points = 0` → contributes **nothing**
- `total_duration`: *currently* the store calls `recalculateDuration()`, which assigns a blank article a fictional `duration = 1` (the "reading time" of empty content). **That's the only reason duration would change at all** — and it's a value computed from nothing. If we drop that call, the blank lesson keeps `duration = null` until its first real save, and contributes **nothing** here too.

I was tying myself in knots trying to increment duration inside the observer — but the honest answer is: a blank lesson has no content, so it has no duration or points yet. Your instinct kills the whole problem.

## The plan

**1. `LessonObserver` — created hook:**

```php
class LessonObserver
{
    /**
     * Keep the course's denormalized counters in sync as lessons are
     * created — increments by the lesson's own values, which for a
     * blank lesson means only the count actually moves.
     */
    public function created(Lesson $lesson): void
    {
        $course = $lesson->course;

        $course->increment('lessons_count');
        $course->increment('total_duration', (int) ($lesson->duration ?? 0));
        $course->increment('total_points', (int) ($lesson->points ?? 0));
    }
}
```

Why still write all three lines if blanks contribute zero? **Symmetry with deletion** — the observer encodes "a lesson's creation adds exactly its own values," so any future creation path (and the module-deletion fix below) can mirror it with subtraction and the math can never go lopsided. For the store path the net effect is exactly what you said: `lessons_count +1`, everything else `+0`.

**2. `LessonController::store` — the whole recalc chain goes:**

```php
DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $module): void {
    $nextOrder = ($module->lessons()->max('order_index') ?? -1) + 1;

    $module->lessons()->create([
        'course_id' => $course->id,
        'title' => 'New Lesson',
        'type' => 'article',
        'order_index' => $nextOrder,
    ]);
});
```

- `$nextOrder` gets the same one-liner cleanup as the module store
- `recalculateDuration()` — **deleted** (blank lesson keeps `duration = null`; the first content save derives it — harmless everywhere: course recalc coalesces nulls, the editor only exposes duration for exams)
- `$module->recalculateStats()` — deleted (blank lesson = 0 points, nothing to add)
- `$course->recalculateStats()` — replaced by the observer

**3. Register** `#[ObservedBy(LessonObserver::class)]` on the `Lesson` model.

## Part 2 (recommended companion): the cascade gap this exposes

Adding `LessonObserver::created` makes an existing gap visible: **deleting a module kills its lessons via the database cascade — which never fires Eloquent events — so `lessons_count` never drops.** (This gap has actually existed since the `ModuleObserver::deleted` change; the module CRUD test's factory-created lesson masked it, and once the observer counts factory creations too, the drift becomes real data.)

The symmetric fix — a `deleting` hook on `ModuleObserver`, firing **before** the cascade:

```php
public function deleting(Module $module): void
{
    $lessons = $module->lessons()->get(['duration', 'points']);

    if ($lessons->isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }

    $course = $module->course;

    $course->decrement('lessons_count', $lessons->count());
    $course->decrement('total_duration', (int) $lessons->sum('duration'));
    $course->decrement('total_points', (int) $lessons->sum('points'));
}
```

Subtracting exactly what creation added (and what the update path's recompute put in) — no negatives, no drift. Course-level deletion stays unaffected (the course row dies with its counters; no observer fires for cascaded modules).

## Verification

`vendor/bin/pint --dirty --format agent` + `CoursesManagementTest` — traced: the lesson CRUD test (two stores → observer → `lessons_count === 2` ✓) and the module CRUD test (factory lesson counted, module deleted → companion decrements → clean) both hold.

Let me think through this carefully and honestly.

**Option A — Chained (lesson → module → course):**

1. **Event-triggered chaining is fragile and surprising.** The ModuleObserver::updated hook would fire on EVERY module update — including renames! `ModuleController::update` (rename) → module->update(title) → updated event → would increment course.lessons_count?! 4. **Semantic opacity.** "Renaming a module might change the course's lesson count" is a bizarre sentence. The chain hides cause-and-effect across two observer files and an implicit event bridge.

2. **Each counter independently tracks the source.** course.lessons_count doesn't depend on modules.lessons_count being right — both are fed from the same lesson event. Drift in one doesn't infect the other.

Great question — this is *the* architectural fork for maintaining denormalized counters, and the answer matters. Let me lay both out concretely, then give you a firm recommendation.

## What each design actually looks like

**Option A — chained (lesson → module → course):** each level only tells its immediate parent, and the parent *re-propagates*:

```
Lesson created
  → module.lessons_count +1
      → (module was updated! → ModuleObserver::updated fires)
          → course.lessons_count +1
```

The catch is that middle hop. Eloquent observers fire on model events — so for the module to "report upward," its `updated` event must carry the propagation. That means `ModuleObserver` needs something like:

```php
public function updated(Module $module): void
{
    if ($module->wasChanged('lessons_count')) {
        $delta = $module->lessons_count - $module->getOriginal('lessons_count');
        $module->course->increment('lessons_count', $delta);
    }
}
```

**Option B — direct (lesson → module AND course):** one event, all effects in one place:

```php
public function created(Lesson $lesson): void
{
    $lesson->module->increment('lessons_count');
    $lesson->course->increment('lessons_count');
}
```

## Why B is the right choice for this app

**1. Your data model is *already* direct.** The `lessons` table carries **both** `course_id` and `module_id` (the double foreign key we've noted since the beginning). The lesson row already knows both ancestors — the observer isn't adding coupling, it's just using what the schema already declares. Chaining would *pretend* the lesson only knows its module, while the schema says otherwise.

**2. Your recompute path is already direct.** Look at `Course::recalculateStats()` — it aggregates `Lesson::where('course_id', ...)` directly, **skipping modules entirely**. The authoritative recompute never goes through the module level. If the observer chained but the recompute went direct, you'd have two different mental models for the same number — and they could disagree. B keeps one philosophy: *course counters are always derived from lessons directly.*

**3. Chained has a nasty failure mode: the intermediate counter becomes load-bearing.** In A, `course.lessons_count` is only as correct as `modules.lessons_count`. Any drift at the module level silently compounds upward. In B, both counters are fed independently from the same source event — a bug in one line breaks one counter, not the chain.

**4. The event bridge in A fires on things it shouldn't.** `ModuleObserver::updated` fires on *every* module update — including a **rename**. The `wasChanged('lessons_count')` sniff guards it, but now every future module update (reorder? title? anything) carries hidden upward-propagation logic, and any code that ever touches `modules.lessons_count` for any reason silently ripples into course counts. Debugging "why did the course count change?" means tracing two observer files and an implicit event bridge. In B, the answer is always: *look at LessonObserver — that's the complete list of consequences.*

**5. The cost B pays is trivial at your depth.** Direct reporting's weakness is fan-out: with a 5-level hierarchy, one event touches 5 tables. You have **two levels**. Two increments. Chaining earns its keep in deep trees; at this depth it's pure overhead.

## When A *would* win — honestly

- **Deep hierarchies** (4+ levels) where direct fan-out gets wide and intermediate aggregates are needed anyway
- **Systems with real domain events** — if you had a `LessonAdded` event bus with explicit handlers, chaining (`LessonAdded` → `ModuleLessonCountChanged` → …) is idiomatic and clean. Eloquent model observers are the *wrong* tool for that pattern; chaining through them is fighting the framework
- **When the intermediate sum is the semantic definition** — "course count = sum of module counts, enforced" — and you want that equation to be structurally guaranteed rather than coincidentally true

None of those describe this app. So: **keep the plan as revised — Option B, the direct two-line observer.** It's more visible, more failure-isolated, consistent with your existing recompute, and matches the schema's own shape.

## Assistant

_Thinking:_

The user asks: should I use an observer or an event listener?

This is a classic Laravel architecture question. Let me think through it carefully in the context of what we're building (the LessonObserver/ModuleObserver pattern for maintaining denormalized counters).

**Observers vs Event Listeners in Laravel:**

**Observer:**
- A class that groups listeners for ALL the Eloquent events of ONE model: `creating`, `created`, `updating`, `updated`, `saving`, `saved`, `deleting`, `deleted`, `restoring`, `restored`, `forceDeleted`
- Registered via `#[ObservedBy]` attribute, `Model::observe()`, or in a service provider
- It's specifically for **Eloquent model lifecycle events**
- Convention: `App\Observers\XObserver`
- Laravel auto-discovers... no, observers need registration (attribute or provider)
- The trait `HasLifecycleCallbacks`... not relevant
- Key: observers are just a convenient *grouping convention* for model events — under the hood they're the same event dispatch system

**Event Listener:**
- Custom events (classes extending `Illuminate\Foundation\Events\...` or plain event classes) + listener classes
- Registered in `EventServiceProvider` (or `AppServiceProvider::boot()` with `Event::listen()`) or auto-discovered listeners
- For **domain events** — things that happen in your application: `LessonPublished`, `CourseEnrolled`, `UserRegistered`
- More ceremony: create event class, create listener class, register mapping (or rely on auto-discovery)
- Can be queued (implement `ShouldQueue`), broadcast, support multiple listeners per event
- Wildcard listeners, event subscribers

**The key insight:** In Laravel, Eloquent observers ARE event listeners — they're just a convention for grouping listeners to model lifecycle events. `$model->created` event fires → Laravel checks if the model has a registered observer → calls `observer->created($model)`. It's the same event system underneath. So the question is really about *which abstraction fits the job*.

**When to use an observer:**
- Reacting to *model lifecycle moments* (created/updated/deleted) regardless of which code path caused them
- Side effects that are intrinsic to the model's existence: denormalized counter maintenance, cache invalidation for the model, default setting, cleanup
- You want it to fire for EVERY creation path (controller, factory, tinker, seeder with inserts bypassing it, jobs)
- One side effect per event, tightly coupled to the model's lifecycle

**When to use custom events + listeners:**
- The thing that happened is a *domain fact*, not a model CRUD moment: "LessonPublished", "ExamCompleted", "StudentEnrolled"
- Multiple, independent reactions to the same occurrence (send email, update leaderboard, log analytics)
- You need queuing (slow side effects shouldn't block the request)
- You want to name the event in business language and decouple emitters from reactors
- The reaction isn't intrinsic to the model — it's application policy

**For our specific use case (denormalized counter maintenance):**

The counter increments are:
1. **Intrinsic to the model lifecycle** — "a module was created" IS the fact; the side effect (course count +1) is a data-integrity concern of the model's existence, not a business policy
2. **Single reaction per event** — one side effect (increment), not a fan-out of unrelated reactions
3. **Must be synchronous and transactional** — the increment MUST commit atomically with the insert (our whole design depends on "delete + increment commit together"). A queued listener would break this — the queue job runs after commit, and if it fails, the counter drifts. This is a decisive point: **counter maintenance must never be queued**, and events/listeners tempt you toward queuing.
4. **Fires for every path** — controller, factory, tinker — observers do this automatically. Custom events would need manual dispatch everywhere (easy to forget a path → drift).

So: **observer is the right tool here.** The observer IS Laravel's purpose-built mechanism for "when this model row is born/dies, keep derived data in sync."

**When would we graduate to events/listeners in this app?**
- The future student side: `LessonCompleted`, `QuizSubmitted` — those are domain facts with multiple reactions (award points to user, update streak, maybe send notification). Those should be custom events.
- If a counter update ever becomes expensive or non-critical (analytics), queue it via a custom event — but never the integrity counters.

Also worth mentioning:
- Observers = same event system, less ceremony, model-scoped convention
- The `#[ObservedBy]` attribute registration we're using is the modern Laravel 11+ way
- Testing: observers fire in tests too (we traced that — factory creations bump counters). With custom events, you'd have to remember to dispatch them in every code path.

Also a subtle point: events/listeners shine when the *emitter* shouldn't know about the *reactor*. In our case, the Lesson model doesn't know about the observer — good decoupling already. But the *event name* for a custom event would be business-level ("LessonCreated") — which is fine but adds a class + registration for zero extra decoupling over the observer.

One more honest consideration: some people argue counter maintenance should be neither — it should be recomputed or handled in the service layer. We've already settled that question (delta maintenance via observers, recompute as authoritative fallback in update/destroy paths).

4. Why observer wins for THIS case (the four reasons, especially the transactional/queuing point)
5. When this app would graduate to events/listeners (student side: LessonCompleted etc.)
6. Verdict: keep observers

Short answer: **for this — observer.** But the question deserves the full reasoning, because the line between them is genuinely worth understanding.

## The hidden truth first: observers ARE event listeners

Under the hood, Laravel has **one** event system. When a model is created, Eloquent fires a `created` event. An observer is just Laravel's *packaging convention* for listening to **all the lifecycle events of one model** — `created`, `updated`, `deleted`, etc. — in a single class. So you're not choosing between two mechanisms; you're choosing between two *abstractions* over the same machinery.

The real question is: **is the thing that happened a "model lifecycle moment" or a "domain fact"?**

| | Observer | Custom Event + Listener |
|---|---|---|
| Reacts to | *"this row was born / changed / died"* | *"this business thing happened"* |
| Fires | automatically, for **every** code path that touches the model | only where you remember to `dispatch()` it |
| Naming | fixed hooks (`created`, `deleted`) | yours, in business language (`LessonPublished`) |
| Ceremony | one class + one attribute | event class + listener class + registration |
| Queuing | synchronous by nature | invites `ShouldQueue` |
| Typical use | data integrity, derived fields, cache cleanup | emails, analytics, notifications, fan-out |

## Why the observer wins for counter maintenance

**1. The trigger is a lifecycle fact, not a business fact.** "A module row was created" is precisely what observers exist for. There's no business decision inside it — no "publish", no "enroll" — just "this row now exists, keep the derived numbers true." The side effect is *intrinsic to the model's existence*, not application policy layered on top.

**2. It fires for every path — which is exactly the property we've been leaning on.** Controller, factory, tinker, a future import command — the observer catches them all. A custom event must be manually dispatched at every creation site; forget one path and the counter silently drifts. (We've already benefited from this: the tests' factory-created lessons get counted, which is *more correct* than the old endpoint-only recalc.)

**3. The decisive one — these side effects must be synchronous and transactional.** Our whole design depends on "insert + increment commit together." The observer fires *inside* the transaction, immediately. Custom event/listener systems exist largely to *escape* the request — queuing, deferring, decoupling slow work. That's the opposite of what an integrity counter needs: a queued counter update that fails leaves drift, and a deferred one means the data is briefly wrong. When you must not queue, the tool that doesn't tempt you to queue is the right tool.

**4. One reaction per event.** Events/listeners shine when one occurrence fans out to *multiple independent* reactors — "LessonCompleted → award points + update streak + send notification." Here it's always exactly one reaction per lifecycle moment. The fan-out machinery would be pure ceremony.

## When this app *should* graduate to events + listeners

The student-facing side, when you build it. Things like:

- `QuizSubmitted` — one fact, several reactions: score the attempt, award user points, update course progress, maybe notify
- `CourseCompleted` — award a badge, email the student, log analytics

Those are **domain facts** — they have business names, multiple unrelated reactions, and some reactions (email, analytics) genuinely *should* be queued. That's the event/listener habitat. And notably, those listeners might themselves *dispatch* to the same counter-maintenance logic — the two patterns stack cleanly.

## Verdict

Keep the plan as is: `LessonObserver` with the two direct increments, registered via `#[ObservedBy]`. It's the purpose-built tool for "keep derived data true when a row is born or dies" — automatic, synchronous, transactional, and impossible to forget to fire. Save events + listeners for the day you have business facts with fan-out reactions.

**Goal:** Apply the observer pattern to the lesson creation lifecycle. A new lesson increments `lessons_count` on **both** its module and its course — directly, count-only, via a `LessonObserver`. The module gains its own `lessons_count` column. The store method's entire recalc chain is deleted.

## 4. `LessonObserver` — the direct, count-only hook

Create via `php artisan make:observer LessonObserver --model=Lesson`:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Observers;

use App\Models\Lesson;

class LessonObserver
{
    /**
     * Keep the denormalized lesson counts in sync as lessons are
     * created — a cheap +1 on both the module and the course.
     */
    public function created(Lesson $lesson): void
    {
        $lesson->module->increment('lessons_count');
        $lesson->course->increment('lessons_count');
    }
}
```

Both increments on hydrated models — `updated_at` touches along the way, preserving the course's "recently edited floats to top" sorting. Fires inside the caller's transaction, so insert + increments commit or roll back together. Catches **every** creation path (controller, factory, tinker).

## 5. `Lesson` model — register

`#[ObservedBy(LessonObserver::class)]` attribute + import, matching the `Module` model's existing style.

## 6. `LessonController::store` — the recalc chain goes

```php
public function store(Course $course, Module $module): RedirectResponse
{
    Gate::authorize('create', Lesson::class);

    DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $module): void {
        $nextOrder = ($module->lessons()->max('order_index') ?? -1) + 1;

        $module->lessons()->create([
            'course_id' => $course->id,
            'title' => 'New Lesson',
            'type' => 'article',
            'order_index' => $nextOrder,
        ]);
    });

    return back();
}
```

Removed, line by line:
- `$nextOrder` — same one-liner cleanup as the module store (drop the redundant `(int)` cast)
- `$lesson =` assignment — return value no longer needed
- `$lesson->recalculateDuration()` — a blank lesson keeps `duration = null` until its first real save (harmless: course recalc coalesces nulls, the editor only exposes duration for exams)
- `$module->recalculateStats()` — blank lesson has 0 points, nothing to add
- `$course->recalculateStats()` — replaced by the observer

The transaction stays: create + two increments must sink or swim together.

## 7. `ModuleObserver` — untouched, per your instruction

One deferred gap, flagged with eyes open: **deleting a module cascades its lessons away at the database level, which never fires the `LessonObserver`** — so `courses.lessons_count` won't drop when a module with lessons is deleted (the module's own counter dies with the row, so that one's moot). No test asserts this today, so the suite stays green. When you're ready, the fix is the `deleting` hook on `ModuleObserver` — pure decrements, no recompute.

- `Lesson::recalculatePoints()`/`recalculateDuration()` — still called by the update path, which derives real values on first content save

I should explain this in the same style as my previous method explanations: big picture analogy, step by step, simple language, tables where useful, "what it deliberately does not do" section, one-breath summary.

Key things to explain:

1. **The big picture**: This renders the standalone lesson editor — the deepest page in the admin. The course editor shows the *outline* (modules + lesson titles); this page shows *one lesson's full content* — the article body or the questions/answers. It's the "open the document" action vs the course editor's "folder view."

2. **Signature**: `edit(Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson)` — triple route model binding with scoped bindings. The URL is `/dashboard/courses/{course}/modules/{module}/lessons/{lesson}/edit`. Three models resolved from the URL; scopeBindings guarantees the chain (lesson belongs to module belongs to course). 404 for mismatches.

3. **Gate check**: `Gate::authorize('view', $lesson)` — instance-level check on the lesson being viewed.

4. **Eager loading with ordering**: `$lesson->load([...])` — same pattern as CourseController::edit, one level deeper: questions ordered by order_index, and nested questions.answers also ordered. Without this, iterating `$lesson->questions` in the map would trigger N+1 queries (one per question for its answers). Two queries total instead of 1+N.

5. **The three props**: course (id + title only — just enough for the breadcrumb/back button), module (id + title — same), lesson (the full payload).

Why are course/module sent at all? The editor page needs:
- `course.id` for the save route (`dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.update` takes course, module, lesson ids) and the back URL
- titles for display/breadcrumb

6. **The lesson payload**:
- `id`, `title`, `type` — identity and the type switch (article vs quiz/exam) that decides which editor variant renders
- `duration` — the interesting conditional: `$lesson->type === 'exam' ? $lesson->duration : null`. Only exams expose duration in the editor! Why? Because for articles and quizzes, duration is DERIVED (computed from word count / question count) — the user never types it. Exams have a manually-set time limit. So the field only gets a value for exams. # The `edit()` Method in LessonController — Explained Simply, Step by Step

## The big picture

If `CourseController::edit` hands the frontend a **folder view** — the whole outline: modules, lesson titles, nothing deeper — then `LessonController::edit` is the moment you **double-click one document and it opens**. You leave the outline behind and enter a single lesson's full working space: the article body in a rich text editor, or the complete question list with answer choices and audio players.

This method's job is to prepare that document for work: fetch the lesson with its entire question/answer subtree, and translate everything into the *shape the editor form expects*. And that translation is the real story here — because the database and the form speak two different languages about one thing: **which answer is correct**.

```php
public function edit(Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson): Response
{
    Gate::authorize('view', $lesson);

    $lesson->load([
        'questions' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index'),
        'questions.answers' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index'),
    ]);

    return Inertia::render('Dashboard/Lessons/Editor', [
        'course' => [
            'id' => $course->id,
            'title' => $course->title ?? '',
        ],
        'module' => [
            'id' => $module->id,
            'title' => $module->title,
        ],
        'lesson' => [ ...the deep payload... ],
    ]);
}
```

---

## Step 1: The signature — a three-model chain from the URL

```php
public function edit(Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson): Response
```

Handles `GET /dashboard/courses/{course}/modules/{module}/lessons/{lesson}/edit` — the deepest route in the app. Three parameters, three route model bindings: Laravel resolves each `{...}` segment to a real model row, or 404s.

The important part is what the chain *guarantees*. Because the route lives inside `Route::scopeBindings()`, the bindings are checked against each other: the lesson must belong to the module, and the module must belong to the course. A URL like `/courses/7/modules/99/lessons/5/edit` where lesson 5 actually lives in module 12? **404 before your code runs.** Like the module `update()` tour, the router verifies the family tree; the controller never has to ask "is this really your lesson?"

## Step 2: The permission check

```php
Gate::authorize('view', $lesson);
```

Instance-level: *"may this admin open this specific lesson?"* — answered by `LessonPolicy::view()`. The same double-lock pattern as everywhere else: route middleware is the gate on the whole dashboard; this stands directly in front of the door.

## Step 3: Clip on the subtree — eager loading, one level deeper

```php
$lesson->load([
    'questions' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index'),
    'questions.answers' => fn ($query) => $query->orderBy('order_index'),
]);
```

The route binding already fetched the lesson *row* — but a lesson row is just a folder label. Its questions and answers live in other tables, and `$lesson->questions` is a **lazy** relationship: it wouldn't touch the database until the moment the code below asks for it.

And the code below asks for it *inside a loop* — once per question, plus each question's answers. Without this `load()`, rendering a 10-question lesson would fire **1 + 10 + 10 = 21 queries** (the N+1 disease). With it: **exactly 2** — one for all questions, one for all answers of all questions. The count is fixed no matter how many questions exist.

The dot notation `'questions.answers'` means "one level deeper": *for every question you're fetching, also fetch all of its answers — batched*. And each closure bolts an `ORDER BY order_index` onto its query — the seat numbers we've built the whole ordering system around. (No `id` tiebreaker anymore, you'll remember — the unique constraints guarantee the order is total.)

After this line, the lesson is a fully-decorated folder: questions clipped inside, answers clipped inside the questions. The rest of the method reads from memory — zero further queries.

## Step 4: Three props — two of them deliberately tiny

```php
'course' => [
    'id' => $course->id,
    'title' => $course->title ?? '',
],
'module' => [
    'id' => $module->id,
    'title' => $module->title,
],
'lesson' => [ ...the big one... ],
```

The editor page needs its ancestors — but only barely:

- **`course.id` and `module.id`** — because the save route (`dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.update`) needs all three IDs in the URL, and the "back to course editor" link needs the course ID.
- **`title`s** — for the breadcrumb display.

No stats, no modules list, no lesson tree — the whitelist principle at every level: the page gets exactly what it displays and uses, nothing more.

## Step 5: The lesson's own fields — with one clever conditional

```php
'id' => $lesson->id,
'title' => $lesson->title,
'type' => $lesson->type,
'duration' => $lesson->type === 'exam' ? $lesson->duration : null,
'article_content' => $lesson->article_content ?? '',
```

- **`type`** decides which editor variant renders — `article` shows the WysiwygEditor; `quiz`/`exam` show the drag-and-drop question list.
- **`duration` is the interesting one.** Only exams receive it; articles and quizzes get `null`. Why? Because duration means different things by type: for exams it's a **manually-set time limit** (the admin types it); for articles and quizzes it's **derived** — computed from word counts and audio lengths, never typed by anyone. The editor form only shows a duration input for exams, so that's the only type that gets a value here. The update method mirrors this exactly (`'duration' => $type === 'exam' ? ... : 0`).
- **`article_content ?? ''`** — the form-input normalization you've seen before: a React controlled textarea needs a string, never `null`. Quiz lessons have no article content at all, so they arrive as `''` — harmless, since the type switch means the article editor never renders for them.

## Step 6: The questions — and the great translation

This is the heart of the method. Each question becomes an array for the form:

```php
'questions' => $lesson->questions->map(function (Question $question): array {
    $answerIndex = $question->answers->search(
        fn (Answer $answer): bool => $answer->id === $question->correct_answer_id,
    );

    return [
        'id' => $question->id,
        'type' => $question->type,
        'question_content' => $question->question_content,
        'answers' => $question->answers->pluck('answer_content')->values()->all(),
        'correct_answer_index' => $answerIndex === false ? 0 : (int) $answerIndex,
        'audio_url' => $question->audio_url
            ? Storage::disk('public')->url($question->audio_url)
            : null,
        'audio_filename' => $question->audio_url ? basename($question->audio_url) : null,
        'audio_duration' => $question->audio_duration,
        'audio_file' => null,
    ];
})->values()->all(),
```

### The star: `correct_answer_id` becomes `correct_answer_index`

Remember the database's way of marking the right answer: the questions table stores **`correct_answer_id`** — a pointer at a specific answer *row* (the circular foreign key from our schema tour). But the frontend form works in **positions**, not row IDs: the answer choices UI is a set of radio buttons, and "which is correct" is just *which button is pressed* — index 2, or 0, or 3.

So this method performs the translation:

1. **`->search(...)`** — walk this question's answers (already in memory from the eager load) and find the position of the one whose `id` matches the stored pointer. Returns the position, or `false` if nothing matched.
2. **The `$answerIndex === false ? 0` fallback** — a quiet piece of armor. `correct_answer_id` is nullable and `nullOnDelete`, so a question *can* exist whose pointer is null or dangling. Rather than crash or complain, the editor opens with the **first choice marked correct**. (Honest footnote: it papers over a data-integrity oddity instead of surfacing it — the pragmatic choice for an editor, but worth knowing it's a fallback, not a truth.)

On save, the reverse translation happens in the controller — index in, pointer out. The two representations never meet except at these borders.

### The other fields, briefly

- **`answers`** — `pluck('answer_content')` collapses each answer *row* into a plain **string**. The answer IDs are deliberately discarded — which makes sense given what you know about the save path: update() deletes and recreates every answer anyway, so their current IDs are worthless to the form. The form speaks in strings and positions; the database speaks in rows and pointers.
- **`audio_url`** — the inline ternary from our `resolveMediaUrl` cleanup: stored relative path → full playable URL for the preview player. Note the **asymmetric round trip**: a full URL goes out, but on save the incoming URL is never *parsed* for identity — retention is keyed by the question's `id` (syncQuestions looks up the old row and keeps its stored path). The URL value coming back is merely a truthy flag meaning "this question still has its audio."
- **`audio_filename`** — `basename()` of the stored path: just the `track.mp3` label for the UI.
- **`audio_duration`** — the seconds Howler measured client-side when the file was uploaded; round-tripped so the duration math survives without re-reading audio.
- **`audio_file` => `null`** — the placeholder that keeps the form shape **symmetrical**. The form's state model has an `audio_file` slot (holding a live `File` object during editing). A `File` can never come *from* the server — it lives on the user's machine — so the slot arrives empty, exactly matching the shape `handleAddQuestion` builds for brand-new questions client-side. One shape, two origins.

## What `edit()` deliberately does NOT do

- **No saving** — `update()` receives the form; `edit()` only lays it out.
- **No stats** — points, durations, counters are irrelevant to editing content.
- **No answer IDs, no lesson points** — the editor can't use them, so they don't ship.
- **No pagination** — a lesson's questions are naturally bounded (a handful), so the whole subtree rides along.

## One breath summary

> *"The URL hands you a verified course → module → lesson chain. The badge check runs. One eager load clips on the entire question/answer subtree — two queries, seat-number order, regardless of size. The editor gets three props: two breadcrumb-sized ancestors, and one deep lesson payload where the database's language is translated into the form's — stored answer-pointer becomes radio-button position (first choice as the quiet fallback), answer rows become plain strings, stored audio paths become playable URLs plus a filename label, and every question arrives with an empty `audio_file` slot so server-loaded and freshly-added questions look exactly alike."*

That's the last read-method in the LessonController. What remains unexplored in this controller is the heavyweight `update()` — the destructive question-rebuild save we've dissected from a distance but never walked line by line. Say the word if you want that tour next.

## 1. Yes — the URL already contains all three IDs. So why pass the models at all?

You're right: `/dashboard/courses/7/modules/12/lessons/55/edit` literally spells out 7, 12, 55. So when the controller receives `Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson`, what did those bindings *add* over just reading the URL?

Three things:

**1. They're not just IDs — they're verified rows.** The URL saying "course 7, module 12, lesson 55" doesn't make it true. Route model binding turns each number into a real fetched row — or a 404 if any doesn't exist. So by the time your code runs, you're not holding "the number 7," you're holding *the actual course row*, guaranteed to exist.

**2. The chain is verified as a family** (because of `scopeBindings()`). Without it, `/courses/7/modules/12/lessons/55` would happily resolve lesson 55 even if it belongs to module 30 in course 9 — three *real* rows that have nothing to do with each other. The scoping makes the URL a *path*, not three independent lookups: module 12 must belong to course 7, lesson 55 must belong to module 12. That's what lets `edit()` trust `$course->id` blindly when building the save URL, and what protects every write endpoint from cross-course tampering.

**3. `$lesson` carries data the URL can't give.** The method immediately does `$lesson->load('questions.answers')` and reads its title, type, content, questions… The binding is what fetched all of that from the database. The URL gave an *address*; the binding gave the *resident*.

So: the IDs in the URL are the *input*; the bound models are the *verified, hydrated output* of turning those IDs into trustworthy data. The method could theoretically re-parse the URL itself, but it would be doing binding's job by hand — with none of the 404 handling, none of the scoping verification, and a lot more code.

```php
]);
```

|---|---|---|
| Map style | arrow fn, one-liner per field | `function` closure, multi-line (because of the search logic) |
| `values()` calls | `->values()->all()` on each nested map | `->values()->all()` at the end only |
| Ancestors | none needed (root resource) | two small breadcrumb props |

## User

why do you include course id and module id in the returning data

---

## Assistant

Sharp question — because the *page component* genuinely uses them, and the reason is worth unpacking.

## The frontend needs all three IDs — but can't get them anywhere else

Look at what the lesson editor page does with those props. From `resources/js/Pages/Dashboard/Lessons/Editor/index.jsx`:

**1. The save endpoint needs the full route signature.** The update route is the deeply-nested one:

```js
router.post(
    route('dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.update', [
        course.id,     // ← 7
        module.id,     // ← 12
        lesson.id,     // ← 55
    ]),
    { ...values, _method: 'put' },
    ...
);
```

Ziggy's `route()` helper needs **every** URL segment filled in — `/dashboard/courses/{course}/modules/{module}/lessons/{lesson}` takes three parameters. Sending only `lesson.id` would fail to build the URL.

**2. The "back to course" link needs the course ID.**

```js
backUrl={route('dashboard.courses.edit', course.id)}
```

The editor's header has a "← Course" back button; it points at the course editor, which is keyed by course ID alone.

**3. The titles are for the breadcrumb/display** — course title and module title shown in the editor header so the admin knows where they are.

## The part your question really exposes — why can't the page just use the URL?

Here's the honest tension: the IDs *are* in the URL — `courses/7/modules/12/lessons/55/edit`. Can't the React component just read them from there? It technically can (Ziggy even exposes `route().params`), and a leaner payload could drop `course`/`module` to just IDs or nothing.

But sending them as **props** is the deliberate Inertia pattern, for three reasons:

**1. Inertia pages are meant to be URL-agnostic.** A page component receives its data as props whether it arrived via full page load, Inertia navigation, or a *partial reload*. Parsing the current URL inside the component couples it to routing details — the prop contract keeps the component saying "I need course, module, lesson" and the controller deciding what those are.

**2. The titles have to come from the server anyway.** The URL contains IDs but *not* the module title for the breadcrumb. Since we're fetching those anyway, the IDs ride along for free — there's no separate saving in sending `module: { id: 12 }` versus `module: { id: 12, title: 'Introduction' }`.

**3. It mirrors every other editor in the app.** The course editor gets `course` (its own resource), the lesson editor gets `course`, `module`, `lesson` — the breadcrumb chain. One convention, applied uniformly.

## What *would* justify trimming them

If you wanted a genuinely minimal payload, the honest version would be:

```php
'course' => ['id' => $course->id],           // title unused? then drop it
'module' => ['id' => $module->id],
```

But checking the frontend: the editor header's back button and the `route()` calls use **both IDs and titles** (the page header shows the module title context). So the current shape is exactly "what the page consumes" — the whitelist principle working as intended, just at the ancestor level.

**One thing your instinct *would* catch, in a stricter design:** `course.title` — is it actually displayed? Let me recall the page… the editor header shows "Lesson" as the form title with "Course" as the back-target label — the course *title* itself may not be rendered anywhere. If so, `title` on the course prop is dead weight and the honest minimal version would send just the ID. That's a one-line trim if you want it.

So the answer in one breath: **the IDs are there because the save URL and back-link need them, the titles are there for the breadcrumb — and shipping them as props instead of parsing the URL is the Inertia convention that keeps page components decoupled from routing.**

The answer is about **what each answer becomes in the payload**:

And `pluck('answer_content')` is Laravel's purpose-built shortcut for exactly that: "extract one column from every item." It's literally equivalent to:

**`pluck` IS a map — it's Laravel's specialized one-column map.** The reason it looks different from the modules/lessons/questions maps is the *shape of the target*:

So there's simply *nothing else to extract* from an answer row. A map that returns `$answer->answer_content` for each would be a wordier way of saying `pluck('answer_content')`. - course → modules: objects (id, title, lessons)
- module → lessons: objects (id, title, type)
- lesson → questions: objects (id, type, content, answers, correct_index, audio...)
- question → answers: **strings**

Each level maps to what the editor needs at that level. The questions need identity (for audio retention on save — `id` is the retention key!) and lots of fields. The answers need neither identity nor fields — just text and position. Position comes free from array order.

So the string-only representation is fully round-trip consistent with the save contract.

## The two shapes

Look at what each transformation produces:

**Questions become objects** — each one needs many fields, so the map builds an array literal:

```php
$lesson->questions->map(fn (Question $question): array => [
```

**Answers become plain strings** — each one contributes exactly one thing, its text:

```php
$question->answers->pluck('answer_content')->values()->all()

// → ['Option A', 'Option B', 'Option C']
```

And `pluck('answer_content')` is *literally* this map, pre-packaged:

```php
$question->answers

    ->all()
```

Identical output, character for character. Writing the long form would just be a wordier way of saying "give me the `answer_content` of each." Laravel's own style guidance — the one from the skill we loaded — says prefer the built-in that communicates intent directly, and `pluck` is that built-in.

## Why answers are only strings — the deeper reason

The asymmetry isn't laziness; it's the payload getting **shallower by design** as you descend the tree, because each level needs less:

| Level | Becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| course → modules | objects (`id`, `title`, `lessons`) | outline needs identity + label + children |
| module → lessons | objects (`id`, `title`, `type`) | outline needs identity, label, type icon |
| lesson → questions | objects (9 fields) | editor needs identity + content + audio + correct-answer pointer |
| question → answers | **strings** | the form needs *text and position, nothing else* |

Recall from the `edit()` tour why answers need nothing else:

- **No `id`** — the save path (`syncQuestions`) deletes and recreates every answer anyway; their current IDs are worthless to the form. (Contrast: the question's `id` *is* kept, because it's the audio-retention key on save.)
- **No "correct" flag** — correctness lives on the *question* as `correct_answer_index`, a position. The answer's role in that is just "being at index 2."
- **Position comes free** — array order *is* the answer's order, because `ORDER BY order_index` sorted them before the pluck.

So an answer's entire contract with the frontend is: *a string, in the right slot*. `pluck` expresses exactly that contract in one word.

## When it would graduate to a `map`

The day an answer needs to become an object — say you add a per-answer `explanation` field, or answers get images, or (in the non-destructive-save redesign we've discussed) answers start keeping their IDs — that's the moment the pluck becomes a map with an array literal, matching its siblings. Until then, `pluck` is not the odd one out; it's the right tool at the right depth.

One small honest footnote on the line as it stands: the `->values()` after `pluck` is technically redundant — `pluck` already re-indexes keys to `0, 1, 2…`. It's there as the same style insurance the course controller applies at every nesting level, so all four tree levels end the same way: `…->values()->all()`. Harmless, and it keeps the pattern uniform.

`updateTitle` is the **quick-rename endpoint** — the inline rename from the course outline. Here's the picture:

## Where it sits in the UX

The course editor's right panel shows the outline: modules with lesson bars inside each one. When you **click a lesson's title** directly on that bar (not navigating anywhere), the title turns into a text input right there:

```js
// CourseContent.jsx — the inline rename flow
const handleSaveLessonTitle = (lessonId, title) => {
    router.patch(
        route('dashboard.courses.modules.lessons.update-title', [
            courseId, moduleItem.id, lessonId,
        ]),
        { title },
        { preserveScroll: true, showProgress: false, only: ['course'] },
    );
};
```

Type the new name, hit **Enter** (or click away → blur), and this endpoint fires. **Escape** cancels without saving. It's the *tiny* edit that shouldn't cost you a page navigation — you rename a lesson the way you rename a file in Explorer, without opening it.

## Contrast with its big sibling, `update`

This is the whole reason it exists. The full `update` method is the heavyweight path: it requires the *complete* lesson content — title, type, article body or the entire question/answer list, duration for exams — validated by `LessonUpdateRequest`, and it **destroys and rebuilds** the whole question subtree. That's the "open the lesson editor and hit Save" path.

But an outline rename doesn't have any of that context. The user is renaming `Lesson 2` in module 3 while its full content sits untouched — and the frontend literally *doesn't have* the content there (the outline payload only carries `id`, `title`, `type` per lesson). Renaming via `PUT update` would force the frontend to first fetch the whole lesson, then echo the entire content back — absurd cost for a one-field change. So the endpoint exists precisely to be the **cheap, narrow door**:

```php
public function updateTitle(Request $request, Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson): RedirectResponse
{
    $validated = $request->validate([
        'title' => ['required', 'string', 'max:255'],
    ]);

    $lesson->update([
        'title' => $validated['title'],
    ]);

    return back();
}
```

One field in, one column written, `back()` for the whisper-quiet partial reload (`only: ['course']`) — the same shape as `ModuleController::update`, its exact twin for module renames.

## The details you already know, applied here

- **Scoped bindings** — the course→module→lesson chain is verified by routing before the method runs
- **No stats** — a title can't change any counter (names don't count toward points), so no recalc, no observer involvement
- **Frontend guards** — the `InlineTitleInput` trims, skips empty/unchanged names, and blocks double-submits, so most junk never reaches the server; the three rules are the real enforcement
- **`back()` not redirect** — the user is mid-outline; they should stay exactly where they are, scroll and open panels preserved

## The two open flaws we've already flagged for it

1. **It's the last inline-validation holdout.** Every other write endpoint now validates through a Form Request class (`CourseUpdateRequest`, `LessonUpdateRequest`, `ModuleUpdateRequest`, both `ReorderRequest`s). This one still uses `$request->validate([...])` in the controller — the exact pattern we migrated away from. The conversion would be a `LessonUpdateTitleRequest` (or a shared rename request) mirroring `ModuleUpdateRequest`.
2. **It's also missing the Gate call.** Notice: no `Gate::authorize('update', $lesson)` — every other write method got one when we added the policies. It's currently protected only by the route middleware + scoped bindings. That's a real gap versus the established double-lock convention, worth fixing whenever we do the Form Request conversion (the request's `authorize()` would be the natural home for it).

So in one breath: **`updateTitle` is the outline's lightweight rename door — one field, one write, stay in place — existing so the frontend never has to round-trip an entire lesson's content just to change its name.** Want me to fold the FormRequest + Gate conversion into the next work session?

# The `update()` Method — The Heavyweight Save, Explained Simply

## The big picture

If `edit()` opens the document, `update()` is the moment you hit **Save**. And this save is unlike any other in the app, for one reason: **the lesson's questions and answers are demolished and rebuilt from scratch on every single save** — the destructive pattern we've dissected from a distance since the beginning.

So think of this method as a **demolition-and-rebuild contractor** who also happens to be a careful archivist. Its full job:

1. Check the badge (Gate)
2. **Photograph the site before demolition** — what audio files exist on disk, what question rows exist in the DB
3. **Demolish** — wipe all questions (answers die by cascade)
4. **Rebuild** — insert the incoming questions/answers fresh from the form
5. **Rescue the archives during the rebuild** — re-attach audio files that the form kept, so they survive the demolition
6. Recompute the derived numbers (points, duration) and refresh the course/module counters
7. **Haul away the orphans** — delete audio files nobody claimed
8. Send the user back to the course editor

Here's the whole thing:

```php
public function update(LessonUpdateRequest $request, Course $course, Module $module, Lesson $lesson): RedirectResponse
{
    Gate::authorize('update', $lesson);

    $validated = $request->validated();
    $type = $validated['type'];
    $previousAudioPaths = $lesson->storedAudioPaths();
    $existingQuestions = $lesson->questions()->get()->keyBy('id');
    $keptAudioPaths = [];

    DB::transaction(function () use ($course, $module, $lesson, $validated, $type, $existingQuestions, &$keptAudioPaths): void {
        $lesson->update([...]);
        $lesson->questions()->delete();
        if ($type !== 'article') {
            $keptAudioPaths = $this->syncQuestions(...);
        }
        $lesson->load('questions');
        $lesson->recalculatePoints();
        $lesson->recalculateDuration();
        $module->recalculateStats();
        $course->recalculateStats();
    });

    $orphanedPaths = array_diff($previousAudioPaths, $keptAudioPaths);
    if ($orphanedPaths !== []) {
        Storage::disk('public')->delete(array_values($orphanedPaths));
    }

    return redirect()->route('dashboard.courses.edit', $course);
}
```

Let's walk it slowly.

---

## Step 0: The rulebook runs FIRST — `LessonUpdateRequest`

Before any line of `update()` executes, Laravel runs the Form Request. Three layers of checking:

**Layer 1 — the badge:** `authorize()` (admin only).

**Layer 2 — the per-field rules.** Note the wildcard machinery — `questions.*.answers.*` reaches *every answer of every question* individually. Each answer: a required string ≤1000 chars; each question: 2–6 answers, a text `required`, an `audio_file` that must be a real mp3/wav/ogg ≤10MB.

**Layer 3 — the `after()` deep checks** — the smart part, enforcing rules that no per-field rule can express:

- **Per-type content:** an article must have non-empty (after tag-stripping) content; a quiz/exam must have at least one question; an **exam** must have a positive time limit
- **The listening-audio requirement:** every listening question must have audio — either a fresh upload *or* saved audio it still references. This is where it gets clever: it looks up `$this->route('lesson')` and checks the **existing DB row** to see whether that question ID already has stored audio. *"You don't need to re-upload; keeping your existing file counts."* This single check is why editing a quiz without touching its audio doesn't force re-uploads
- **The correct-answer pointer:** the index must actually point inside the answer list

Key detail: `questions.*.id` is `nullable` — the form sends `id: null` for new questions, an ID for retained ones. The validation doesn't care; the rebuild treats them nearly identically anyway.

If any layer fails → **422**, the user never leaves the editor, and errors flow into the react-hook-form error tree keyed by the same paths (`questions.2.audio_file`).

---

## Step 1: Photograph the site

```php
$validated = $request->validated();
$type = $validated['type'];
$previousAudioPaths = $lesson->storedAudioPaths();
$existingQuestions = $lesson->questions()->get()->keyBy('id');
$keptAudioPaths = [];
```

Two snapshots, taken **before** anything changes:

- **`$previousAudioPaths`** — every audio file path on disk belonging to this lesson's questions (the manifest). Once the question rows are deleted, the database forgets these paths — so we must write them down now, or we'd never know what to clean up (or what exists to keep).
- **`$existingQuestions`** — the current question rows, keyed by ID. This is the **audio rescue registry**: when a question comes back with `id: 34` and no new upload, we'll look here to find 34's stored audio path and re-attach it to the new row.

`$keptAudioPaths = []` — the empty claim ledger. During the rebuild, every audio file that survives gets checked in here.

## Step 2: Demolish and rebuild — inside the transaction

```php
DB::transaction(function () ... {
    $lesson->update([
        'title' => $validated['title'],
        'type' => $type,
        'article_content' => $type === 'article' ? ($validated['article_content'] ?? '') : null,
        'duration' => $type === 'exam' ? (int) $validated['duration'] : 0,
    ]);

    $lesson->questions()->delete();
```

First the lesson's own row updates in place (title, type — and note the mirrored conditionals from `edit()`: article content only for articles, duration only meaningful for exams).

Then **the demolition**: one statement deletes every question row. The answers die instantly with them — **not** by PHP loop, but by the database's `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Zero events fire (mass delete), which is also why no observer interference happens here.

Why demolish at all? Because the form sends a flat list of questions with no reliable "which changed" information — the **id churn** problem we've covered. The rebuild is the brute-force answer: wipe, reinsert, done.

```php
    if ($type !== 'article') {
        $keptAudioPaths = $this->syncQuestions(
            $lesson, $validated['questions'] ?? [], $existingQuestions,
        );
    }
```

The rebuild — only for quiz/exam. (An article has no questions at all; validation already guaranteed its content exists.)

## Step 3: `syncQuestions` — the builder with the archive desk

Per incoming question, in order:

1. **Resolve audio**, three ways:
   - New `UploadedFile` → `store('lessons/audio', 'public')` → fresh file, fresh path
   - No new file, but `id` + `audio_url` present → look up the **old row** in the registry → reuse its stored path, **and check it into the ledger** (`$keptAudioPaths[]`)
   - Otherwise → null (validation already guaranteed this can't happen for listening questions)
2. **Insert the question row** with `order_index` = array position (fresh dense seats — no parking dance needed since the old rows are gone)
3. **Insert each answer** (strings → rows, position → `order_index`)
4. **Back-patch the pointer**: `correct_answer_id` = the ID of whichever answer sits at `correct_answer_index` — the circular FK's two-phase tango, exactly like seeding

Return: the ledger of claimed paths.

## Step 4: Recompute the numbers

```php
    $lesson->load('questions');
    $lesson->recalculatePoints();
    $lesson->recalculateDuration();
    $module->recalculateStats();
    $course->recalculateStats();
```

Fresh questions are in the DB, but the relation cache still holds the *deleted* set — `load('questions')` re-reads. Then the derivation rules you know: points = words/10 (article) or questions×10 (quiz/exam); duration = reading time / quiz audio math / exam keeps its limit. Finally the module and course counters get the **authoritative full recompute** — the corrector that overwrites any drift, never stacking with the observer increments.

## Step 5: Haul away the orphans — after commit

```php
$orphanedPaths = array_diff($previousAudioPaths, $keptAudioPaths);
if ($orphanedPaths !== []) {
    Storage::disk('public')->delete(array_values($orphanedPaths));
}
```

The manifest minus the ledger = **files nobody claimed** — a deleted question's audio, or audio replaced by a new upload. They die *after* the transaction commits, the safe ordering from the `destroy()` tour: worst case is orphaned files on disk, never a dangling reference.

One honest edge: retention is keyed by **question `id` + truthy `audio_url`**. If the frontend ever drops an ID, that question's audio silently loses its claim — unclaimed file deleted, new row points at nothing. Fragile, but the frontend is disciplined about it.

## Step 6: Redirect

Back to the course editor — done editing, leave the standalone editor, see the refreshed outline.

## One breath summary

> *Rulebook first: per-type content requirements, listening-audio presence (existing saved audio counts), pointer sanity. Then: photograph the site — manifest of audio paths, registry of question rows. Transaction: update the lesson row, demolish every question (cascade kills the answers), rebuild from the form — rescuing audio by ID from the registry and checking survivors into a ledger — then recompute points/duration and re-author the module/course counters. After commit: manifest minus ledger = orphaned files, hauled away. Redirect to the outline.*

## The known costs (the redesign threads)

- **ID churn** — question/answer identities are disposable, blocking any future "student answered #57" feature
- **Full rebuild per save** — one typo fix = N+M inserts
- **The fragile retention key** (id + truthy URL)

The non-destructive alternative we've sketched: diff incoming questions by `id` — update in place, insert new, delete missing; audio retention becomes *keeping the row* instead of re-attaching paths; IDs become stable. That's the big one waiting when you want it.

## Why `update()` isn't like CourseController's (the honest answer)

The course editor's split works because the **outline is always persisted** — "Add Module" immediately creates a row, renames PATCH immediately, every right-panel action is its own tiny endpoint. The left panel ("Save Course") only ever saves metadata.

The lesson editor took the opposite philosophy: it's a **one-shot draft form**. Questions live in client-side state (never persisted until Save), so there's no per-question endpoint to PATCH — the whole form must arrive in one request. And once a *batch* of questions arrives with no reliable "which changed" information, delete-and-rebuild is the brute-force shortcut. **The destructiveness (item 1) is a direct consequence of the batch save (item 3).** Fix the shape, and the destruction has nowhere to live.

## The proposed architecture — split the save, diff the content

**Endpoint 1 — `update` (left panel only):** title, type, exam duration. Plain JSON `PUT` (no files in metadata!). Mirrors `CourseController::update` exactly.

**Endpoint 2 — `updateContent` (right panel):** article body *or* the question list. Multipart `PUT .../lessons/{lesson}/content` (audio files ride here). This replaces `syncQuestions` with a **non-destructive diff sync**:

```
For each incoming question:
  has id + row exists  → UPDATE in place (type, text, order_index, audio swap)
  id null              → INSERT (answers fresh, correct_answer_id back-patched)
Registry rows not in payload → DELETE (answers cascade; audio → obsolete list)
```

- **Audio becomes the course cover-image pattern** — a retained question *keeps its row*, so it keeps its file with zero bookkeeping. New upload → store new, delete obsolete *after commit*. The entire manifest/ledger dance (`$previousAudioPaths`/`$keptAudioPaths`) disappears.
- **Answers get stable IDs too** — `edit()` ships `{id, content}` objects; the sync diffs them the same way, so "student picked answer #57" becomes possible. `correct_answer_index` stays positional on the wire, resolved to `correct_answer_id` after the answer sync.
- **Order writes use the established park-then-place** within each parent (lesson→questions, question→answers) — the unique constraints demand it, same as module reorders.

**Items 2 & 4 — one derivation rulebook, finally.** Right now backend and frontend *disagree*: backend says words/150, the UI preview says words/200 and "30s per question + audio." The plan makes the `Lesson` model the single source and mirrors the same constants in the UI preview:

| | Proposed formula |
|---|---|
| Article duration | `max(1, ceil(words / 200))` (the UI's existing constant wins; backend currently 150) |
| Quiz duration | `Σ(30s per text question + max(30s, audio) per listening)` → minutes |
| Exam duration | the entered time limit (unchanged) |
| Article points | `max(1, ceil(words / 10))` (unchanged) |
| Question points | text = **10**; listening = **10 + ceil(audio_duration / 60)** — "content + one point per minute of audio" |
| Lesson points | sum of the above |

Both endpoints re-derive points/duration after saving (a type switch on the left panel changes the derivation branch, so metadata saves re-derive too), then run the module/course recalc as the authoritative corrector.

**Frontend changes:** zod schema gets answer objects; `AnswerChoicesInput` holds `{id, content}` pairs (strings for display); `LessonContent` gains a "Save Content" button in its section header (the `SectionHeading` action slot — same place "Add Question" lives); `LessonInformation`'s preview constants updated to match the canonical rules, plus a points stat for parity.

**Tests:** rework the lesson CRUD test to the two endpoints + new coverage: in-place update keeps question/answer IDs, delete-missing cascades, audio swap safe-ordering, formula assertions, reorder-parking under the unique constraint. (Testing skill gets read before writing them.)
